items.title: There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?
items.blurb: Aldebaran looks for all the world like the brightest member of the Hyades star cluster. It isn't — and discovering why changes the way you look at constellations.

items.title: Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?
items.blurb: A biblical mystery, an ancient Egyptian inscription and a "ring of fire" solar eclipse 3,200 years ago hold clues to when Ramesses the Great ruled.

items.title: Russia is developing a nuclear space weapon, US intelligence report finds
items.blurb: A new report by the the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency discusses the threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space — including Russia, which is developing a nuke-carrying satellite.

items.title: A Triple Star System 'That Shouldn't Exist,' Only 28 Light-Years from Earth
items.blurb: Astronomers have found a triple star system in our neighborhood that has defied the odds. It shouldn't really exist, according to astronomers' understanding of stellar evolution and common envelopes. Yet, there it is.

items.title: NASA Honor Awards Ceremony Recognizes Employees at Stennis Space Center
items.blurb: Employees contributing to NASA’s mission at the agency’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, were recognized during the center’s Honor Awards ceremony on Nov. 18. Presenting the awards were Christine Powell, NASA Stennis center director, and Jeremy Parsons, the agency’s Artemis program manager responsible for management and oversight of NASA’s initiative to return

items.blurb: This collage shows 49 drill holes captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover as of November 2026.

items.title: NASA’s Curiosity Mars Rover Collects Samples
items.blurb: This Nov. 16 collage shows 49 drill holes captured by NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover as of November 2026. Each hole represents a sample collected from rocks on the Martian surface; Curiosity’s drill, located on the end of its robotic arm, drops pulverized rock samples into instruments in its belly that analyze their composition. items.title: ISS astronauts look down on the snow-capped Himalayas | Space photo of the day for Nov. 20, 2026
items.blurb: The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station.

items.title: Sound Waves From Sunspots Launch Fiery Plasma Jets Across the Sun
items.blurb: It feels like every week for the past few months we’ve been reporting on more research regarding the temperature difference between the Sun’s surface and its corona. This week is no exception, with a new paper in The Astrophysical Journal detailing the formation and tracking of around two hundred jet-like bursts of plasma from the surface known as “dynamic fibrils.” They serve as another piece of the puzzle of why the Sun’s outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than its surface.

items.title: Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’
items.blurb: When links in a communication network go down, messages can get routed in a loop. Computer scientists now know that four simple network structures are to blame. The post Network Researchers Nail Down Theory of ‘Perfect Resilience’ first appeared on Quanta Magazine

items.title: This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers
items.blurb: Some binary stars end up sharing a common envelope of gas, as the primary star draws material away from its companion. The envelope exerts drag on the stars and they can spiral toward each other. In some cases, this creates an eruption or explosion called a luminous red nova. For the first time, astronomers got to observe one of these in real time.

items.title: I got to tour SpaceX's Starfactory facility in Starbase, Texas, and what I saw blew my mind
items.blurb: SpaceX invited media on an unprecedented behind-the-scenes tour of its Starfactory facility, where it manufactures and assembles both stages of its massive Starship rocket.

items.title: Artemis astronauts on the moon will see Earth upside down
items.blurb: Artemis astronauts will explore the moon's south pole, so Earth will appear "upside down" to them. Read more strange things the astronauts will experience here. The post Artemis astronauts on the moon will see Earth upside down first appeared on EarthSky .

items.title: Mystery space object moves in strange ways
items.blurb: 1998 KY26 is a mystery space object that accelerates in ways that gravity alone can't explain. A new study suggests light photons from the sun are the cause. The post Mystery space object moves in strange ways first appeared on EarthSky .

items.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
items.blurb: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.

items.title: Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds
items.blurb: We’ve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes aren’t good at telling the full windy story - they can’t tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.

items.title: I handpicked every Star Trek Blu-ray discounted on Amazon for Black Friday 2026 that I think is worth buying right now
items.blurb: From The Original Series through The Next Generation to Starfleet Academy, beam up our favorite Black Friday 2026 Star Trek deals available at Amazon.

items.title: Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured
items.blurb: An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity, and that verifies Einstein's greatest theory.

items.title: SpaceX Dragon cargo capsule heads home to Earth from the ISS
items.blurb: SpaceX's 35th Dragon cargo mission undocked from the International Space Station today (Nov. 20), starting its journey home to Earth.

items.title: What are heat pumps and how much do they cost?
items.blurb: The government wants more homes to have heat pumps to cut fossil fuel use and drive down energy bills.

items.title: Tucana the Toucan is home to the Small Magellanic Cloud
items.blurb: Tucana the Toucan is an easy-to-spot constellation in the Southern Hemisphere. Just look for the Small Magellanic Cloud and a bright star cluster. The post Tucana the Toucan is home to the Small Magellanic Cloud first appeared on EarthSky .

items.title: Wildlife conservation cash targets ex-colliery sites
items.blurb: The project aims to create and restore habitats for amphibians and lizards at sites in Yorkshire.

items.title: Mysterious Mercury is about to get a visitor - after spacecraft's eight-year epic voyage
items.blurb: The mission is set to give us our best ever view of Mercury - the closest planet to the Sun.

items.title: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
items.blurb: Astronomers have traced mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole to a massive pair of stars whose colliding winds appear to create dense clumps of material. These clouds may eventually feed the black hole, revealing a surprising connection between stellar activity and the growth of cosmic giants.

items.title: The Stormy Southwest Pacific
items.blurb: Tropical Cyclone Xavier launched the basin’s storm season with a bang.

items.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
items.blurb: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.

items.title: Voyager 1 team, unbowed by communications glitch, celebrates epic 1-light-day distance milestone
items.blurb: The Voyager 1 team celebrated the probe's big distance milestone on Thursday (Nov. 19), even while dealing with a communication anomaly that recently cropped up on the probe.

items.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
items.blurb: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Here's why it mattered.

items.title: On this day in space! Nov. 19, 2005: Japan's Hayabusa spacecraft makes 1st-ever liftoff from surface of an asteroid
items.blurb: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft made the first liftoff from an asteroid. Here's why it mattered.

items.title: The view from the tower: Watch Starship come in for chopsticks catch in epic slo-mo video
items.blurb: A new set of slo-mo videos gives us a tower's-eye view of the first-ever catch of a Starship upper stage, a milestone SpaceX achieved last weekend.

items.title: No more asteroid landing: Engine trouble forces Japan's Hayabusa2 probe to change plans
items.blurb: Japan's space agency has decided to switch destinations and objectives for the final act of its Hayabusa2 asteroid mission, due to problems with the spacecraft's ion thrusters.

items.title: Oil firm fined for breaking environmental rules hundreds of times
items.blurb: Ten charges involved oil, cyanide and other pollutants entering local waterways.

items.title: Rain breaks up Earth’s natural sunshades
items.blurb: EarthCARE sheds light on one of the processes that leads to the breakup of vast, bright clouds that help keep our planet cool – with rain emerging as a key driver.

items.title: Watch live: Hera’s first images of post-impact asteroid Dimorphos
items.blurb: A little more than four years ago, humans moved an asteroid, as NASA’s DART spacecraft impacted a body called Dimorphos. Now the European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft has arrived at that same asteroid to find out what happened next. Join the Hera team on the evening of Wednesday 25 November as they share the first close-up images of this historic transformed space object.

items.title: Will Voyager 1 ever be closer than 1 light-day from Earth again?
items.blurb: The Voyager spacecraft get closer to Earth for a few months every year. Will Voyager 1 cross back under the 1 light-day distance? The post Will Voyager 1 ever be closer than 1 light-day from Earth again? first appeared on EarthSky .

items.title: Seven-spacecraft observatory to study plasma universe
items.blurb: ESA Member States have selected Plasma Observatory as the agency’s next medium-class mission. Its seven coordinated spacecraft will track how the Sun’s energy moves through Earth’s magnetic shield, across different scales of distance and time.

items.title: NASA Astronaut Reid Wiseman Attends Ravens vs. Saints Game
items.blurb: NASA astronaut and commander of the agency’s Artemis II mission, Reid Wiseman, a Baltimore native, takes a selfie with fans at an NFL game between the New Orleans Saints and the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium, Sunday, Sept. 20, 2026, in Baltimore.

items.title: X-ray technique advances temperature measurements under extreme pressure
items.blurb: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) have advanced the ability to measure temperatures in materials subjected to extreme pressures at the National Ignition Facility (NIF), providing new insights into how materials behave under conditions relevant to national security and high-energy-density physics.

items.title: Parasite protein expands understanding of how mitochondria build their ribosomes
items.blurb: Mitochondria are essential components of the cells of most organisms, including humans. They are often referred to as the cell's powerhouses because they produce the energy needed for cellular functions. However, mitochondria originally evolved from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by other cells in the distant past.

items.title: Mapping the microbes' arms race with viruses at planetary scale
items.blurb: Microbiomes are complex ecosystems, in which bacteria and archaea are constantly interacting with, and infected by, viruses. These viruses can significantly impact microbiome processes, not only by killing their host but also sometimes by temporarily providing additional capabilities to their host. As many viruses have not been grown in a lab, connecting them to their natural hosts has been difficult. A new bioinformatics toolkit and database are now available to help researchers make those associations at an unprecedented scale.

items.title: El Niño created a skiers' paradise in Chile—now it's Sierra Nevada and southern Rockies' turn
items.blurb: El Niño has a reputation for being a skier's dream, bringing lots of snow to California's Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies. Tahoe-area resorts were already seeing the effects in mid-November 2026 as several feet of snow fell and some resorts prepared to open early for the season. But El Niño's supercharged precipitation can spell trouble, too.

items.title: Can Psychedelics Improve Decision-making?
items.blurb: A new study suggests they free the mind from prior biases

items.title: Practical organ-on-a-chip platform helps assess the toxicity of environmental chemicals
items.blurb: Among the thousands of chemicals used in daily life, toxicity information is available for only a small fraction. Much of this information comes from high-dose animal studies, which are costly, time-consuming and limited by species differences.

items.title: New sources of neurotoxin linked to algal blooms uncovered in Florida and Kansas
items.blurb: Researchers have identified two previously unreported strains of freshwater cyanobacteria capable of producing a potent neurotoxin that poses risks to people, pets, wildlife and water resources and that some scientists suspect may have contributed to previous animal deaths.

items.title: Bumblebees challenge long-held beliefs about brain size and intelligence
items.blurb: Bigger brains mean greater intelligence, or so conventional wisdom goes. After all, humans have much larger brains than most other animals and are generally considered the planet's most intelligent species.

items.title: Is it genuine love—or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts
items.blurb: Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation—these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don't want to let that person out of your sight.

items.title: Clean energy choices shape environmental impacts beyond greenhouse gas emissions
items.blurb: The burning of fossil fuels such as coal, gas and oil is the primary driver of climate change, but clean energy strategies to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions do not systematically alleviate other environmental problems. In fact, some pathways add pressure on natural resources like land, water and minerals.

items.title: Witnessing generosity from low-income donors more likely to elicit giving from observers, research finds
items.blurb: Billionaire Warren Buffett announced this month he will donate $5.47 billion to four foundations associated with his family ahead of Thanksgiving. Similarly, various students in club organizations throughout Kansas are collecting food items to give to hungry families for the holiday.

items.title: Spiders, beetles and one garage alligator: Largest study to date reveals wildlife sharing our indoor spaces
items.blurb: An international team of researchers is revealing the largest study to date detailing the wide range of insects, arachnids and other organisms that live in homes and other indoor environments across the United States and Canada. The researchers have compiled a database with more than 20,000 entries spanning more than 2,000 species found in these indoor ecosystems.

items.title: Deep Venture: A new class of ocean exploration vehicle developed
items.blurb: Researchers have a new capability for exploring some of the least understood regions of the ocean. Developed by Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) in collaboration with NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, Deep Venture is a next-generation autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) for deep-ocean research, capable of supporting a wide range of scientific missions, from shallow coastal waters to the deepest places on Earth. It can withstand extreme pressure, rated for depths of up to 11,000 meters (about 6.83 mi), or full ocean depth.

items.title: Anthropic researcher says Claude solved math's greatest riddle
items.blurb: A mathematician at AI company Anthropic said Friday that he had used the firm's Claude chatbot to prove the Riemann hypothesis, a problem that has eluded mathematicians for more than 160 years.

items.title: A new way to extract oxygen from lunar soil could support bases on the moon
items.blurb: Computer chip manufacturing and lunar exploration seem like completely different worlds. Yet our latest research suggests the two may be more closely connected than expected.

items.title: Theory explains how fusion plasmas enter a state of improved energy confinement, solving a 40-year puzzle
items.blurb: Nuclear fusion promises a source of energy by combining light atomic nuclei, the same process that powers the sun. To achieve fusion on Earth, scientists must heat a gas to extreme temperatures, creating a charged state of matter called plasma. Keeping this plasma hot and stable long enough for fusion energy production is one of the main challenges facing the technology.

items.title: U.K.'s nature health check doesn't stack up in wildlife's favor—but volunteers are collecting plenty of crucial data
items.blurb: As nature declines over time, it becomes easier to normalize an increasingly impoverished environment.

items.title: More worried, yet more hopeful: The paradox of young people's climate action
items.blurb: New research from NIHR School of Public Health Research, published in the Lancet Planetary Health, provides new insights into how taking action on climate can impact young people's climate change distress, mental health and well-being.

items.title: Killer whales became fearsome predators long before scientists thought
items.blurb: Killer whales, or orcas, are among the ocean's most formidable predators, hunting everything from fish and seals to other whales. But how and when these members of the dolphin family evolved into such effective hunters has long been something of a mystery.

items.title: A Physician Explains GLP-1s’ Biggest Potential Side Effect: A Rare But Serious Eye Condition
items.blurb: What is the risk for the millions of people worldwide who take GLP-1 medications?

items.title: US bill aiming to boost clean energy could backfire
items.blurb: The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is a gamble that speeding up permits for energy projects would help renewables more than fossil fuels – but many environmentalists have doubts

items.title: How desert biocrusts respond to changing snow cover
items.blurb: In the desert, winter snow may seem like a temporary visitor, but its effects can last long after the snow melts. By supplying water to dry ecosystems, snowfall helps sustain biological soil crusts (biocrusts), thin living layers on the soil surface that play important roles in desert ecosystems.

items.title: Excitons mimic light in atom-thin material, confirming decade-old quantum prediction
items.blurb: Combining their skills in theory and experiment, Yale researchers have observed for the first time a type of energy-carrying composite particle move in a highly unexpected way. It's a finding that could lead to advances in quantum technologies, solar energy, LEDs and other optoelectronic technologies. The work is published in Nature Physics.

items.title: Researchers trace shifting pulsation modes in δ Scuti star KIC 4737720
items.blurb: Stars in the night sky may look calm and unchanging, but some are in fact constantly "vibrating." Just as a musical instrument can sound several notes at once, a star can pulse in several modes simultaneously. By measuring minute changes in a star's brightness, astronomers can read these stellar vibrations and, in turn, probe the physical processes at work inside it.

items.title: Venus-like conditions reveal how minerals could preserve traces of ancient water
items.blurb: Venus is one of the most inhospitable environments in our solar system, with surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead and atmospheric pressure nearly 100 times greater than Earth's. Yet its surface may preserve clues to a time when the planet looked much more like Earth.

items.title: Tokyo's hidden methane: Survey pinpoints nearly 100 hot spots
items.blurb: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) has been the poster child of climate change, but another culprit could be flying just under the radar. Methane is a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential approximately 84 times greater than that of CO₂ over a 20-year period. Fortunately, methane remains in the atmosphere for only about a decade, and reducing its emissions could provide rapid climate mitigation effects.

items.title: Male bumblebees contribute to nest care, challenging view that they only mate
items.blurb: For decades, researchers have assumed male bumblebees' contribution to hives consisted mainly of DNA. However, a new study finds that the males actually help incubate baby bumbles, and that with males' assistance, hives thrive. The study, published in the Royal Society Open Science journal, quantifies the beneficial effects of having male babysitters in the hive.

items.title: Misinformation perception shapes support of democracy in Australia
items.blurb: A new study by Adelaide University researchers has found that the more often people perceived they had encountered misinformation, the less positive their views of Australian democracy tended to be. The experience-sampling study from the School of Psychology asked 123 eligible voters to track their perceived exposure to misinformation in the lead-up to the 2025 Australian federal election and measured whether this exposure influenced their attitudes and emotions toward the election.

items.title: Low-viscosity lavas reveal a key to Mars's past
items.blurb: Since 2021, the Mars Perseverance rover has been roaming Jezero Crater, gathering details about the red planet's geology and hints about its past. On its journey, the rover took close-up images of the Séítah formation, a nearly 4-billion-year-old layer of rock at the base of the crater.

items.title: Mobile streaming habits offer global societal insights
items.blurb: Researchers from the University of the Sunshine Coast observed how a total of 959 consumers in the U.S., South Korea and Germany used mobile streaming services.

items.title: A star's last gasps: ALMA reveals a giant gas ring and budding hourglass around a star in transition
items.blurb: Stars like our sun don't die quietly. In their final act, they swell into red giants, shed their outer layers into space and leave behind a glowing, often strikingly sculpted cloud of gas called a planetary nebula. That transformation is thought to take only a few thousand years, a blink in the life of a star, so catching one in the act is rare.

items.title: Anthropic mathematician claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
items.blurb: The Riemann hypothesis is one of the most difficult problems in mathematics, having stood for 167 years. It may have just been settled with the help of AI

items.title: Low oxygen at high altitudes may protect honey bees from deadly parasites
items.blurb: Honey bees (Apis mellifera) are the most important managed pollinator of agricultural crops globally. A study published Nov. 19 in the open-access journal PLOS Biology by Huoqing Zheng at Zhejiang University, Hangzhou, China, and colleagues suggests that parasitic mites causing honey bee colony collapse have less reproductive success at high altitudes.

items.title: We found a seaweed that hadn't been spotted in 90 years—and discovered vast underwater forests
items.blurb: A tangle of long, caramel-colored seaweed. That's what botanist A.H.S. Lucas found in 1935 while conducting research near Lord Howe Island, a World Heritage–listed site known for its unique biodiversity. After collecting some large adult specimens of this previously unidentified seaweed, Lucas named it Sargassum howeanum.

items.title: What Do Peahens Really Want?
items.blurb: A new chapter in evolutionary biology argues that animals’ bright colors and patterns are about more than just sex

items.title: US, Russia and China look set to block ban on autonomous weapons
items.blurb: More than 70 countries are ready to begin negotiations on prohibiting lethal autonomous weapons, but large militarised nations are expected to obstruct efforts to agree a ban

items.title: A Rope Bridge Camera Just Discovered a New Species of Howler Monkey
items.blurb: These monkeys can now travel further afield

items.title: Keto diet slashes liver fat by 67% in just 4 months
items.blurb: A new clinical trial found that the ketogenic diet dramatically outperformed Mediterranean and low-fat diets in reducing liver fat and improving metabolic health, even when participants lost similar amounts of weight. After just four to five months, about half of those following keto no longer met the criteria for prediabetes, while their liver fat dropped by an average of 67%.

items.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
items.blurb: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

items.title: This simple habit is linked to a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's
items.blurb: Reading for pleasure may have surprisingly powerful benefits for the brain, with studies linking it to better memory, reduced stress, improved mental health, and a lower risk of dementia. Researchers highlight findings that just five minutes of fiction can reduce stress by up to 20%, while reading has also been associated with a 33% lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

items.title: Unexpected stone tools from Israel raise questions about cultural evolution
items.blurb: Ancient humans in the eastern Mediterranean first began producing advanced stone blades 100,000 years before the tools became widely used, indicating that new technologies weren't automatically adopted by communities

items.title: My grandmother was a seal
items.blurb: Many Irish families believed they descended from selkies. Their stories reveal the violence and grief in our kinship with nature - by Jordan Lee Borgman Read on Aeon

items.title: Galactic shock: Discovery challenges our understanding of the Milky Way's structure
items.blurb: A University of Sydney Ph.D. student has uncovered evidence that the Milky Way is unusual in terms of where its new stars are born compared with nearby galaxies.

items.title: A two-layer flat lens uses nanoscale pillars to guard against unwanted reflections
items.blurb: Researchers in the Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (SEAS) have engineered an advancement in metasurface design and processing that now includes a built-in, intentionally designed antireflective coating—a potentially critical step toward greatly expanding the incorporation of metasurfaces into practical devices.

items.title: Dark Eden author Chris Beckett on how sci-fi needs ‘surface plausibility’
items.blurb: Chris Beckett, author of Dark Eden, November's read for the New Scientist Book Club, talks to Alison Flood about how he wrote his Arthur C Clarke award-winning novel

items.title: For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard
items.blurb: A study of more than 10,000 college students found that exercising regularly may be more important for mental health than pushing yourself through intense or lengthy workouts. Students who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety a year later, suggesting that consistency could be a key ingredient in protecting mental well-being.

items.title: The secret maths problems hidden throughout Japan
items.blurb: Hundreds of years ago, Japanese mathematicians enshrined their work onto painted wooden tablets displayed throughout the country. Columnist Jacob Aron explores the history of the practice of sangaku and the effort to digitally preserve these artefacts

items.title: UN climate talks enter crunch time with no deal in sight
items.blurb: The U.N.'s COP31 climate talks enter their endgame Friday, with countries sharply divided over a draft deal lacking any mention of planet-heating fossil fuels, threatening to push the negotiations into overtime.

items.title: Fiona the hippo dies after failed effort to remove swallowed hat
items.blurb: World-famous hippopotamus Fiona has died after several failed attempts by vets to remove a woolly hat that she accidentally swallowed, the Cincinnati Zoo announced Thursday.

items.title: Nature's multilayered defenses against crop pests and viruses revealed
items.blurb: Researchers from the University of Nottingham, in collaboration with Syngenta and Keele University, have discovered how a commercial barley hybrid uses three complementary natural defenses to protect itself against aphids and the damaging viruses they spread. The findings could help breeders develop crops with stronger natural protection against pests and diseases.

items.title: The BepiColombo spacecraft is finally entering orbit around Mercury
items.blurb: After an eight-year voyage towards the sun, the BepiColombo spacecraft can finally begin its mission to unpick the many mysteries of our solar system's smallest planet

items.title: computor: AI tutor as a programming learning aid
items.blurb: Artificial intelligence is now capable of writing entire computer programs. This poses a challenge for university education. How can students still learn to program for themselves if an AI can do the work for them? Students should be able to use AI tools effectively, but they must also understand how programs work and how to troubleshoot errors. At the Institute of Theoretical and Computational Physics at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), a team led by Christopher Albert has developed the "computor" learning platform for this purpose. The system is already being used in teaching and is available to the public.

items.title: Powerful new weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half
items.blurb: A powerful experimental weight-loss drug helped people with knee osteoarthritis lose about 25% of their body weight at the highest dose, while roughly two-thirds experienced at least a 50% reduction in knee pain. The findings suggest retatrutide could transform treatment for millions suffering from painful arthritis, although its ability to prevent further joint damage remains unknown.

items.title: How nature-based solutions are failing informal settlements
items.blurb: New research from UCT says nature-based solutions for climate adaptation must move beyond participation to power-sharing partnerships that recognize lived experiences and relationships with nature.

items.title: Extreme weather poses growing risks to global oil and natural gas shipping, new IEA report finds
items.blurb: Extreme weather events are posing significant risks to international oil and natural gas shipping, with the potential to damage critical infrastructure, disrupt major trade routes and threaten energy security, according to a new IEA report.

items.title: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
items.blurb: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree. The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins.

items.title: AI virtual cell technology could reveal how genetic changes and drugs alter cells
items.blurb: Today's artificial intelligence models can predict whether someone with a genetic change will develop a disease, but cannot answer two critical questions: Why did the disease occur, and how do we design a treatment?

items.title: Building structured-light systems in three dimensions
items.blurb: Structured light has become an important tool across modern optics. By shaping properties such as amplitude, phase, polarization and spatial mode, researchers can create light fields with capabilities beyond those of conventional laser beams. These engineered light fields are finding applications in communications, imaging, sensing, optical computing and quantum photonics. However, many structured-light systems still rely on multiple discrete optical components that require careful alignment and occupy significant space.

items.title: Innovative technology offers a bold new vision for monitoring ocean health
items.blurb: On an early October morning, as MBARI's research vessel Paragon left Moss Landing with three robots loaded on its deck, Monterey Bay was showing off.

items.title: New mondo grass species found in Yunnan
items.blurb: Botanists have described a new Ophiopogon species from the Yunnan Wenshan National Nature Reserve in southeastern China. They named it Ophiopogon longiscapus for its unusually long flowering stalk, or scape.

items.title: A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best
items.blurb: A major review involving more than 30,000 people found that three antidepressants, including Lexapro and Cymbalta, may be more effective than Prozac at maintaining improvements in depression symptoms. However, limitations in the research and a lack of truly long-term data mean scientists still cannot say which antidepressant is best.

items.title: Organizational science offers new lens for studying extremism
items.blurb: Accepting the Republican nomination for president in 1964, Barry Goldwater declared, "I would remind you that extremism in the defense of liberty is no vice!" His statement illustrates how the cause being defended can shape judgments about the actions taken in its name.

items.title: New study: The last bird to go extinct in NZ has lessons for saving other species
items.blurb: The last bird to go extinct in Aotearoa New Zealand was a tiny wren that disappeared from a small island off the southern tip of Rakiura Stewart Island around 1972.

items.title: Climate communication that resonates must be based on empathy
items.blurb: Climate change is a global reality, but people often encounter it through different local realities. For some, it enters everyday life through social media feeds, news reports, scientific findings and public discussion. For others, it is through water scarcity, food insecurity, floods, heat waves, wildfires or the loss of a home or a loved one.

items.title: NEPTUNE poised to replace Navy's global weather model, improving forecasts over open ocean
items.blurb: The U.S. Naval Research Laboratory-developed Navy Environmental Prediction sysTem Utilizing a Nonhydrostatic Engine, known as NEPTUNE, is poised to become an operational Navy weather prediction capability, providing improved environmental forecasts to support naval operations around the globe.

items.title: Putting Google's AI hurricane model to the test
items.blurb: A week before Hurricane Melissa slammed into Jamaica last fall, the forecast models couldn't agree on where it was headed or how strong it would get. One got it right—an AI model from Google DeepMind, which called both the storm's path and its Category 5 strength.

items.title: AI companions could help reduce loneliness, study finds
items.blurb: AI companions could help reduce loneliness by creating a greater sense of belonging and improving self-esteem, according to new research from Durham University Business School.

items.title: Q&A: Making hydrogen peroxide without using precious metals
items.blurb: Hydrogen peroxide is used in many industrial processes, with several million tons of it being manufactured worldwide every year. Whereas the standard production method requires rare precious metals, chemists from Rutgers University–Newark in the US and the University of Bonn have now described an alternative technique that does away with these metals, making it potentially cheaper and more sustainable. Their findings have now been published in the journal Nature Communications. In the following interview, the authors describe the technology.

items.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
items.blurb: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.

items.title: Can AI save peer review from AI?
items.blurb: Academic journals are flooded with papers. At publishing giant Elsevier, the number of submissions rose 56% in just three years—from 2.7 million in 2022 to 4.2 million in 2025. That's a lot more papers. And peer reviewers, who generally volunteer their time, were already stretched thin.

items.title: Mercury-bound X-ray telescope delivers first images after eight years in space
items.blurb: The first data from a U.K.-built instrument heading to Mercury have provided observations of one of the brightest X-ray sources in the sky from aboard the ESA/JAXA BepiColombo spacecraft in the inner solar system.

items.title: Lifting weights reduces muscle loss from obesity drugs
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03751-3 Resistance exercise could help middle-aged and older individuals to maintain muscle mass and strength during weight-loss treatment.

items.title: Spatial organization of a SPINK1-associated tumor-stromal ecosystem links metabolic remodeling to immune restriction in bladder cancer
items.blurb: Spatially organized tumor-stromal interactions contribute to metabolic remodeling and immune suppression in bladder cancer (BLCA). Using spatial transcriptional programs to define single-cell states, we identified a niche comprising SPINK1-high epithelial cells (E2) and TPM2-high cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) (C1). SPINK1 promoted tumor growth and myofibroblastic CAF programs, with EGFR and TGF-{beta} signaling implicated in tumor-CAF communication. Inferred metabolic reactions and spatial metabolite distributions supported a candidate circuit linking tumor-derived lactate to CAF oxidative metabolism and glutamine provision, followed by tumor glutamine utilization for reductive carboxylation and fatty acid synthesis. SPINK1 perturbation altered extracellular glutamine and lactate concentrations. Predicted chemokine interactions implicated C2/C3 CAFs in T cell recruitment, whereas the E2-C1 niche exhibited checkpoint and exhaustion-associated features. RHCG-positive tumor regions contained higher proportions of TOXCXCR4 cells among CD3 T cells, suggesting a possible association between ammonia handling and T cell dysfunction. In vivo, Spink1 loss attenuated tumor progression, increased cytotoxic CD8 T-cell infiltration, and enhanced tumor control during PD-1 blockade. These findings identify a spatially organized tumor-stromal niche associated with metabolic cooperation and immune restriction, supporting SPINK1 as a candidate therapeutic target in combination with immunotherapy.

items.title: The tumor suppressor role of the KRAS proto-oncogene in metastatic pancreatic cancer.
items.blurb: KRAS is the most frequently mutated proto-oncogene in human cancers. Progression to advanced disease is frequently associated with allelic imbalance of the KRAS locus with gain of the mutant allele and loss of the wild-type allele through clonal and sub-clonal loss of heterozygosity (LOH). While a large body of literature has focused on the effects of allelic imbalance on oncogene addiction through gain of the mutant allele, the role of the wild-type KRAS proto-oncogene in malignant progression has not been fully elucidated. To capture this phenomenon, we developed a first-in-class somatic mosaic and lineage tracing genetically engineered mouse model (smGMLT) of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma allowing for real time in vivo tracing of Kras-LOH. Longitudinal characterization of the smGMLT demonstrated the presence of a strong evolutionary bottleneck towards the selective loss of the wild-type allele at metastatic sites. Cross species analysis leveraging research autopsies and surgical specimens revealed that KRAS-LOH is associated with metastatic dissemination and shorter overall survival. Transcriptomic analysis through single-cell RNA sequencing uncovered a conserved phenomenon whereby KRAS-LOH is paralleled by an immune evasive phenotype through loss of the tumor-cell interferon response and reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration. In line with this evidence, orthotopic transplants of isogenic tumor populations differing for the Kras allelic status demonstrated that only cancer cells with Kras-LOH are are able to form tumors in immune competent animals. Restoration of the wild-type allele abrogates tumorigenesis in KrasLOH transplants in immunocompetent through activation of the TBK1-IRF axis. Altogether, these studies demonstrate that the KRAS proto-oncogene is a functional tumor suppressor in pancreatic cancer exerting its function through interferon-mediated, cell-extrinsic modulation of the tumor immune microenvironment.

items.title: CELL-X: A Single-Cell Transcriptomics Framework for Cell-Type and Disease-State Prioritization of Type 2 Diabetes Risk Genes
items.blurb: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci associated with Type 2 Diabetes (T2D), yet pinpointing specific causal genes and their relevant cellular contexts remains a critical bottleneck. To address this gap, we developed CELL-X, a novel computational framework systematically integrating fine-mapped genetic evidence with high-resolution single-cell transcriptomics and disease progression dynamics. Utilizing a custom out-of-memory processing engine, we analyzed an integrated human pancreatic islet atlas of 245,878 cells without forced data downsampling. We evaluated 37 genetically supported T2D candidate genes, quantifying cell-type relevance via a max-scaled Cell Relevance Score (CRS). Disease-associated transcriptional dynamics were subsequently incorporated using a Disease Relevance Score (DRS) based on heterogeneous expression shifts across normal, prediabetic, and T2D metabolic states. CELL-X successfully identified beta cells as the dominant disease-relevant cellular context and prioritized established causal genes, including SLC30A8, GLIS3, GCK, and TCF7L2. Validation against a 30-gene benchmark demonstrated exceptional target recovery and significant metabolic pathway enrichment. Furthermore, rigorous statistical null modeling confirmed this prioritization is driven by true biological variance rather than background transcriptomic noise. Ultimately, CELL-X provides a highly scalable, robust framework for generating biologically informed hypotheses in complex polygenic disease research.

items.title: SNP2Cluster-Py: A pathogen-agnostic, context-aware framework for Core SNP and transmission-cluster analysis
items.blurb: Whole-genome sequencing enables high-resolution identification of genetically related pathogen isolates, but genomic similarity alone does not establish epidemiologically meaningful transmission. We developed SNP2Cluster-Py, an open-source Python framework that separates context-aware Core SNP clustering from the subsequent application of epidemiological and temporal criteria. The software accepts a precomputed pairwise Core SNP-distance matrix and user-configured metadata and supports analysis of all eligible isolates in a single context, as well as sequence-type, geographical, epidemiological and ordered composite contexts. Within each context, authoritative Core clusters are defined as connected components of an SNP-threshold graph; K-means assignments and silhouette widths are retained as exploratory diagnostics only. We evaluated the workflow using 172 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from six neonatal-surveillance hospitals in South Africa, a focused 36-isolate single-hospital subset from the same surveillance dataset, and 168 Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage isolates from Ghana. In the full K. pneumoniae dataset, ST-only analysis assigned 141 isolates to Core SNP clusters, whereas Facility + ST analysis assigned 134, demonstrating how facility stratification can remove cross-facility genomic connections. In the single-hospital subset, both contexts assigned 30 of 36 isolates to five Core clusters, and Facility analysis retained 23 isolates in four temporally compatible clusters. In the pneumococcal dataset, ST-context analysis assigned 114 isolates to 38 Core clusters, which were characterised across sampling locations and time through Community analysis. SNP2Cluster-Py therefore provides a reproducible framework for adapting genomic clustering to specific surveillance questions while maintaining a clear distinction between genomic relatedness, analytically inferred transmission clusters and confirmed direct transmission. SNP2Cluster-Py v1.1.2 is available under the Apache License 2.0 through GitHub and Zenodo.

items.title: Learning RNA secondary structure from chemical probing with MXfold2
items.blurb: Training RNA secondary structure predictors is limited by scarce reference annotations, even as chemical probing produces abundant nucleotide-level measurements. These measurements inform pairing states without identifying base-pairing partners. Here we extend MXfold2, which combines neural and thermodynamic folding scores, to learn from probing profiles and predict RNA secondary structures from sequence alone. We introduce three training objectives. One learns from probing-assisted target structures. The other two use implicit maximum-likelihood estimation to pass surrogate gradients from reactivity-ranking and likelihood losses through discrete folding. Simulations, RNAgym measurements and external structural tests show improved chemical agreement and gains in exact base-pair prediction when chemical supervision is combined with structural pretraining and replay. Probing profiles can thus broaden the range of RNAs that inform sequence-only structure prediction, including RNA populations with few complete structure annotations.

items.title: NeuroSim: a clinically informed multi-disorder EEG simulator with personalized pattern injection and AI-driven neurological modeling
items.blurb: Deep learning for electroencephalography (EEG) based neurodiagnostics is constrained by the limited availability of labeled clinical recordings. Datasets covering Alzheimers disease (AD), Parkinsons disease (PD), schizophrenia (SCZ), epilepsy (EPI), and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are scarce, demographically narrow, and heterogeneous across acquisition sites, while privacy requirements restrict data sharing. Existing EEG simulators typically address a single disorder or trade biological interpretability for statistical fidelity. This study presents NeuroSim, a simulation framework that generates synthetic multichannel EEG with user-controlled injection of disease-specific patterns across five disorders and multiple severity levels. A physiologically motivated baseline generator produces band-limited rhythms, event-related potentials, artifacts, and hierarchical subject-level and trial-level variability. Disease patterns are introduced through region-specific and severity-specific spectral modulation that encodes established biomarkers, including posterior alpha suppression in AD, motor beta enhancement in PD, and spike-wave discharges in EPI. An interactive interface exposes montage, sampling rate, duration, artifacts, stimuli, affected regions, and severity, and exports signals with reproducible metadata. The simulated signals reproduced the expected biomarker directionality under spectral, topographic, and multivariate statistical analysis. A convolutional-attention classifier trained on simulated data reached 95.3 to 96.8 percent hold-out accuracy, and post hoc explainability analyses produced class-separable embeddings with attributions concentrated on pathophysiologically expected electrodes. Application of the analysis pipeline to recordings from the Temple University Hospital EEG Corpus confirmed compatibility with heterogeneous clinical data. In subject-level augmentation experiments on real clinical EEG, supplementing real training data with NeuroSim samples increased classification accuracy from 91.6 to 94.5 percent for AD versus healthy controls and from 90.9 to 94.0 percent for PD versus healthy controls, exceeding the improvement obtained with conventional signal-level augmentation. NeuroSim is released as open-source software to support augmentation, benchmarking, and explainable artificial intelligence in neurological diagnostics.

items.title: Identification of SAMD4B as a Centrosome-Associated Regulator of the Sonic Hedgehog Signaling Pathway
items.blurb: Background: Many protein-protein interactions are required for the assembly and function of primary cilia, microtubule-based organelles critical for the Sonic hedgehog (Shh) signaling pathway and, in turn, for embryonic development and tissue homeostasis. However, our understanding of this complex process remains incomplete. Methods: To identify new regulators of primary cilia formation or function, we carried out proximity labeling experiments and compared interactomes under ciliogenesis-restrictive and permissive conditions. Using an unbiased strategy, we selected candidates that were tested functionally by siRNA-mediated depletion or gene editing, in combination with gene expression analysis and various microscopy techniques, using either vertebrate cell lines or zebrafish as model systems. Results: We demonstrate that one of our identified candidates, protein SAMD4B, is associated with the centrosome and is required for Shh signaling in NIH3T3 cells and eye development in zebrafish. Our data implicate defective ciliary recruitment of Shh pathway regulators ARL13B and SMO as a plausible mechanism underlying the SAMD4B-mediated regulation of Shh signaling. Conclusions: Together, our data identify a previously unrecognized link between SAMD4B, a protein known to be associated with cytoplasmic RNA condensates, and ciliary signaling.

items.title: Autoinhibition and conformational activation regulate cell-wall anchoring of the bacterial type IV pilus machinery
items.blurb: Type IV pili are widespread bacterial nanomachines that mediate adhesion, motility and host interactions, yet the molecular mechanism coordinating assembly of their outer-membrane channel with attachment to the bacterial cell wall has remained unknown. Here, we show that the conserved PilQ-associated protein TsaP functions as a conformationally regulated envelope adaptor linking secretin assembly to cell-wall anchoring. A crystal structure of full-length TsaP, integrated with structural, biophysical and functional analyses, reveals a compact autoinhibited conformation in which the N-terminal LysM domain is sequestered against the protein core. Comparative structural analyses support a mechanism in which PilQ association remodels TsaP, exposing the LysM domain for peptidoglycan binding. Together, our findings support a mechanistic model in which PilQ-dependent conformational activation of TsaP couples secretin assembly to cell-wall anchoring, providing a framework for understanding the regulated integration of type IV pilus machineries within the bacterial envelope.

items.title: Detection of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium and discrimination of vanA and vanB genotypes by VITEK MS Prime MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry and machine learning
items.blurb: Rapid identification of vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium (VREfm) and discrimination of resistance mechanisms (VanA and VanB) are critical for appropriate antimicrobial therapy and infection control, particularly during outbreaks. Matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS), combined with machine learning, has emerged as a promising tool for this purpose. We evaluated whether MALDI-TOF mass spectra acquired on VITEK MS PRIME, combined with machine learning, could provide this information. Spectra from 388 from clinical and rectal surveillance samples (135 vancomycin-susceptible (VSEfm), 138 vanA and 115 vanB VREfm) were processed with Clover MSDAS, and four algorithms (partial least squares-discriminant analysis (PLS-DA), linear and polynomial support vector machines (SVM-L and SVM-P) and random forest (RF)) were trained to discriminate VSEfm from VREfm and VanA from VanB isolates. Model performance was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation and using independent set of characterized E. faecium isolates from routine practice. Pairwise and triplet ensembles of these algorithms were also assessed. In the test set, PLS-DA was the best individual classifier for VSEfm versus VREfm (balanced accuracy, 78.9%), and the ensemble of PLS-DA and linear SVM reached 80.7%. Validation within routine isolates confirmed the models robustness, achieving 100% correct classification. Discrimination of VanA from VanB was more accurate: 93.2% with RF and up to 97.1% with ensembles. Identical sequence types were found among susceptible, VanA and VanB isolates, indicating that classification was not driven by clonal lineage. MALDI-TOF MS combined with machine learning is a promising, low-cost tool for VREfm screening and vanA/vanB differentiation.

items.title: Treg- and CD8-Specific PD-1 Deficiency Reveals That CD8⁺ T Cell-Intrinsic Signaling Uniquely Restrains Pressure Overload Inflammation and Heart Failure
items.blurb: Aims: PD-1 signaling limits cardiac remodeling and heart failure (HF). Whether this protection depends on PD-1 signaling intrinsic to CD8 T cells or on regulation by other immune populations, including regulatory T cells (Tregs), remains unclear. Methods and results: Using transverse aortic constriction (TAC), we studied global PD-1-knockout (KO) mice with or without CD8 T cell depletion, CD8 T cell-specific (PD1KOCD8), and Treg-specific PD-1-KO mice. We assessed left ventricular (LV) remodeling, genomic profiles, immune infiltration, and the therapeutic impact of C-X-C motif chemokine receptor 3 (CXCR3) blockade. CD8 T cell depletion abolished TAC-induced left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, fibrosis, and dysfunction of global PD-1-KO mice. PD1KOCD8 mice had normal baseline cardiac function but, after TAC, showed reduced survival, worse LV dysfunction and fibrosis, and greater immune cell infiltration. CD8 T cells from PD1KOCD8 mice showed increased activation and proliferation, with increased production of cytotoxic molecules, such as IFN-{gamma} and granzyme A, both at baseline and after TAC. Post-TAC transcriptomics revealed enhanced inflammatory pathways and suppressed metabolic pathways in PD1KOCD8 hearts. TAC also increased LV CXCR3+CD8+ T cell accumulation and CXCL9/CXCL10 expression in PD1KOCD8 mice. CXCR3 neutralizing antibody treatment reduced LV CD8+ T cell accumulation and attenuated cardiac dysfunction. In contrast, Treg-specific PD-1 deficiency did not alter baseline or TAC-induced cardiac remodeling. Conclusions: CD8 T cell-intrinsic PD-1 restrains TAC-induced HF, whereas Treg-intrinsic PD-1 is dispensable. CXCR3-dependent recruitment drives pathological CD8 T cell accumulation, identifying PD-1/CXCR3 axis as a key regulator of CD8 T cell-mediated cardiac injury.

items.title: Sex-dependent rewarding effects of nicotine in mice are prevented by the atypical antipsychotic aripiprazole
items.blurb: Nicotine stands amongst the most commonly used drugs in contemporary societies. Preparations for nicotine consumption range from traditional tobacco products (smoking) to modern electronic cigarettes (vaping). However, its rewarding and reinforcing effects vary as a function of dose and biological sex. In addition, few treatments exists for nicotine use disorders Here we sought to characterize the effects of nicotine on anxiety in the elevated plus maze (EPM) and reward in the conditioned place preference (CPP) paradigm in male and female mice and test the hypothesis that aripiprazole, a partial dopamine agonist, prevents nicotine-induced CPP. Nicotine effects were tested at 0.25, 0.5 and 1 mg/kg. The highest dose reduced basal locomotion in both males and females exposed to the open field and reduced open arm exploration in males in the EPM. Thus, the apparent anxiogenic-like effect is confounded by a reduction in basal exploratory activity. In the CPP paradigm, nicotine 0.5 mg/kg served as a reward conditioned stimulus in males, but not females. Finally, aripiprazole (0.1, 1 and 10 mg/kg) consistently prevented the acquisition of nicotine (0.5 mg/kg) CPP in males. These findings show a sexually dimorphic effect of nicotine in mice and suggest the antipsychotic aripiprazole as a potential pharmacological approach for reducing nicotine reward.

items.title: Centimeter-sized Human Vitreous Organoids from Pluripotent Stem Cells
items.blurb: The vitreous, the largest intraocular tissue, provides a transparent light path and maintains the intraocular homeostasis. The reconstitution of the vitreous in vitro or in vivo remains an unsolved biomedical challenge. Here, we discovered a common feature, the "growth edge", constituted primarily of fibroblasts and their secreted proteins in human and mouse vitreous development. By leveraging the transforming growth factor beta signaling, we then generated centimeter-scale vitreous-like organoids (VOs) through stepwise differentiation from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs). The VOs exhibited striking similarity to human vitreous in terms of physical transparency, vitreoretinal interface, molecular composition, biological profiles and regenerative transplantability. Lines of evidence supported that fibroblasts are the key cell hub for vitreous development. Finally, VOs with a transthyretin (TTR) mutation recapitulated the vitreous phenotypes of human patients with vitreous amyloidosis. Together, vitreous organoid technology opens avenues for future studies of human vitreous development, disease modeling, and regenerative therapeutics for a broad spectrum of human vitreoretinal diseases.

items.title: Unraveling molecular mechanisms for specification of blastomere identity and neural fate in the annelid Capitella teleta
items.blurb: The evolution of central nervous systems remains highly debated as we incorporate data on developmental mechanisms in understudied taxa. Yet how this process occurs in the third major bilaterian clade called Spiralia (e.g., annelids, mollusks) remains inconclusive. Using blastomere isolations, we previously found that in the annelids Capitella teleta and Platynereis dumerilii, ectodermal blastomeres fated to generate the brain and ventral nerve cord can form neural tissue after being isolated. However, in C. teleta, nerve cord formation can be inhibited or rescued by other blastomeres. To ascertain the molecular mechanisms underlying this process, we performed RNAseq on isolated blastomeres in C. teleta at the 8-, 16- and 32-cell stages and found differential expression of components of canonical Wnt signaling across the animal-vegetal axis when conditional neural specification is occurring. Furthermore, asymmetrical localization of TALE and FOX transcripts along the embryonic axis suggests a role in establishing blastomere identity, as observed in mollusks. Our data suggest the integration of an ancestral gene regulatory network of FOXQ2-cWnt and lineage-specific genes during early development, linked to the emergence of spiral cleavage.

items.title: Membrane progesterone receptors spatially organize and partner with ABHD2 to mediate metabolic signaling
items.blurb: Membrane progesterone receptors (mPRs) mediate rapid hormone responses, yet how they engage effectors remains poorly understood. Here, we reveal a spatially regulated partnership between mPRs and the lipid hydrolase ABHD2 that provides a mechanistic basis for the early steps of non-genomic progesterone signaling in mammalian cells. Agonist stimulation promotes mPR-dependent accumulation of predominantly intracellular ABHD2 at the plasma membrane and enhances its association with mPRs. Although human ABHD2 binds progesterone, its phospholipase A2 activity requires partnership with mPRs and an intact catalytic site. ABHD2 deletion disrupts agonist-induced metabolic signaling in hepatic and muscle cells and affects glucose homeostasis in obese mice. Together, these findings uncover a conserved receptor-hydrolase signaling mechanism in which spatially regulated association and receptor-dependent enzymatic activity emerge as defining features of non-genomic steroid signaling.

items.title: A GPNMB-associated lysosomal program tracks neurodegeneration across the DAM continuum
items.blurb: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) profoundly remodel microglial states, yet how the heterogeneity of disease-associated microglia (DAM) relates to neurodegeneration remains incompletely understood. Using a progranulin (PGRN) and TMEM106B-deficient mouse model recapitulating key features of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), including lysosomal impairment, we demonstrated that CSF1R inhibition reduced microgliosis yet accelerated neurodegeneration, suggesting a protective microglia contribution under lysosomal stress. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed that increasing Gpnmb expression within DAM was associated with a shift from immune and inflammatory processes toward a lysosomal, autolysosomal, and lipid-catabolic program. Across disease models, engagement of the GPNMB-associated program correlated with neurodegeneration. Consistently, A{beta}-driven models with limited neurodegeneration exhibited prominent DAM activation but comparatively limited GPNMB expression and engagement of this program. The GPNMB-associated program was TREM2-dependent, while loss of TREM2 signaling under lysosomal stress was associated with exacerbated neuronal damage. Conversely, lysosomal rescue markedly reduced the GPNMB-associated program, demonstrating its reversibility. CSF proteomics identified a convergent lysosomal and microglial signature across models overlapping with alterations reported in human FTD. Together, GPNMB marks reversible, TREM2-regulated lysosomal transcriptional adaptation along the DAM continuum that scales with lysosomal burden and neurodegenerative severity, consistent with a potentially protective microglial response under lysosomal stress.

items.title: An H3K9me3high epigenetic state constrains neuronal activation and synaptic remodeling in the aged dentate gyrus
items.blurb: How epigenetic states shape neuronal responses to experience and memory remains poorly understood. Here, using a quantitative, single-event approach, our study identifies a subset of neurons that accumulate H3K9me3 (H3K9me3high neurons) via the methyltransferase Suv39h1, specifically in the dorsal dentate gyrus (dDG) of aged mice. FACS coupled to RNA-seq showed that dDG-H3K9me3high neurons express a transcriptional state that fails to induce plasticity machinery despite engaging memory-stabilization programs. Using our novel NucleuSynapse-Tag approach, we found that H3K9me3 accumulation interferes with neuronal activation and synaptic remodeling in response to behavioral stimulation in aged mice. Further, genetically inhibiting Suv39h1 to lower dDG-H3K9me3high numbers improved memory in aged mice. Together, these findings reveal a region- and cell-type-specific epigenetic mechanism linking impaired neuronal responsiveness to age-related memory decline, providing mechanistic insight into the therapeutic potential of targeting Suv39h1.

items.title: Widespread SARS-CoV-2 brain infection after intranasal challenge leads to innate and anti-viral immune response and interference with neuronal function in K18-hACE2 mice
items.blurb: Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2), the causative agent of the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, often spreads to the brain in K18-hACE2 transgenic mice after intranasal challenge, leading to widespread neuronal infection. Despite frequent reports of this phenomenon, the effects of SARS-CoV-2 infection on neurons have not yet been fully investigated. Therefore, using the K18-hACE2 mouse model, we performed an in-depth in situ characterisation of brain changes associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection, with a specific focus on infected neurons and glial cells. We challenged mice intranasally with the SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant at a low dose of 100 PFU/mouse and investigated the brains 6 or 7 days later with a combination of morphologic (light microscopy, transmission electron microscopy), virologic (RT-qPCR), and bulk multi-omics (transcriptome, proteome, metabolome, lipidome) approaches. In our model, SARS-CoV-2 infected only neurons, where it replicated, as confirmed by ultrastructural analysis and supported by multi-omics results. Despite high viral burden, productive SARS-CoV-2 infection of neurons elicited only minimal degenerative changes and rare cell death; however, the transcriptome suggested possible functional alterations. Besides the previously reported mild inflammatory response, neuronal infection initiated an innate immune and antiviral response as well as a mild glial response. In conclusion, the K18-hACE2 model of intranasal SARS-CoV-2 Delta infection allows to study the pathomechanisms associated with viral neuronal infection without overt cell death, contrasting with other neurotropic viruses.

items.title: Dual C5aR1 and C5aR2 deficiency uncouples neutrophilic inflammation from antibacterial host defense
items.blurb: Streptococcus pneumoniae is a major cause of bacterial pneumonia and mortality worldwide. While host defense critically depends on complement activation, how C5aR1 and C5aR2 orchestrate pulmonary antibacterial immunity remains unclear. We identified alveolar type II epithelial cells as a local source of C5 and confirmed increased susceptibility of C5-deficient mice to infection. Combined C5aR1/C5aR2 deficiency abolished C5a-induced lung inflammation but paradoxically exacerbated neutrophil accumulation during pneumococcal infection, exceeding that observed in either single-receptor deficiency. Despite their abundance, neutrophils exhibited impaired bacterial clearance, excessive extracellular trap formation, accompanied by aggravated lung injury and mortality. CITE-seq revealed profound neutrophil and macrophage dysregulation, identifying distinct neutrophil subclusters with defective antimicrobial programs, increased cell death and altered inflammatory signatures, consistent with functional exhaustion. Thus, C5aR1 and C5aR2 exert complementary, partially non-redundant functions that couple neutrophil recruitment to antimicrobial competence, prevent excessive inflammation, and preserve effective pulmonary host defense.

items.title: Tetrodotoxin-resistant NaV1.8 contributes to action potential conduction in a population of mouse and human vagal nerve fibers
items.blurb: Axonal action potential (AP) conduction is dependent on voltage-gated sodium channels (NaV1s). AP conduction in the vagus nerve (which contains afferent and efferent fibers) is essential to its reflex regulation of most visceral organs. The nine isoforms of NaV1s show diverse expression patterns in vagal neurons. In rodent vagus nerves, multiple NaV1 isoforms contribute to AP conduction, with NaV1.7 playing an essential role in ~70% of fibers. Here, we investigated the contribution of tetrodotoxin-resistant (TTX-R) NaV1.8 towards vagal AP conduction ex vivo. We tested two structurally different NaV1.8-selective inhibitors, A803467 and PF01247324 and their effects on electrically evoked C-fiber compound action potentials (CAPs) along mouse and human vagus nerves. Tetrodotoxin completely abolished mouse and human vagal CAPs. Nevertheless, both A803467 and PF01247324 caused a concentration-dependent decrease in the C-fiber CAPs in mouse and human vagus nerves. The selectivity of both drugs was tested in NaV1.8 knockout mice. A803467 but not PF01247324 significantly decreased NaV1.8 KO vagal CAPs, indicating that PF01247324's inhibition of wildtype vagal CAPs was solely mediated by NaV1.8, and that A803467 caused inhibition via NaV1.8-mediated and non-NaV1.8-mediated mechanisms. In further studies of wildtype mice, NaV1.8 inhibition following incubation with NaV1.7-selective inhibitor PF05089771 showed no further decrease in mouse vagal CAP, demonstrating that NaV1.8-dependent inhibition affects fibers also sensitive to NaV1.7-dependent inhibition. These data suggest that TTX-sensitive NaV1.7 and TTX-R NaV1.8 cooperate to conduct APs along a select population of vagal nerves. Axonal NaV1.8 inhibition could be utilized to treat aberrant vagal nerve activity in visceral organ diseases.

items.title: Velocity-dependent friction in a simple two-oscillator system. I. Phase amplitude coupling
items.blurb: Cortical gamma oscillations often arrive in bursts locked to the phase of slower theta waves, a pattern called theta gamma phase amplitude coupling (PAC). PAC is linked to memory and altered in epilepsy, but most models tie it to particular cells or circuits. We start from a generalized Langevin equation, an equation of motion for a few collective variables in which friction and random forces stand for the unobserved neural activity, and let its stiffness and friction depend on the state. Expanding them to first order in the theta and gamma variables yields ten possible interaction terms; only the two friction type terms change gamma energy and produce PAC, and depending on the term and its sign the gamma bursts sit at the peak, trough, rising or falling phase of theta. We study a gamma friction that follows theta velocity as a simplified example. Because the time integral of theta velocity is theta coordinate, the gamma amplitude rises and falls with theta coordinate as exp(gvvx{theta}/2). The fluctuation dissipation theorem turns noise and damping into a theta effective temperature, and the PAC strength becomes a closed form function of one dimensionless number, kappa , that combines the coupling with this temperature. Without fitted parameters, this prediction accounts for 51,095 simulated records (R2 = 0.993) and for the median PAC of 5,160 combinations of coupling and damping (R2 = 0.989). The coupling also drives gamma out of equilibrium: its kinetic temperature grows far above the one inferred from its response. All coefficients enter linearly so that they can, in principle, be estimated from recordings by linear regression. A companion paper shows that the same number sets the distance to a stability boundary.

items.title: Velocity-dependent friction in a simple two-oscillator system. II. Regions of stability
items.blurb: In Part I, a gamma friction that follows theta velocity produced theta gamma phase amplitude coupling (PAC) whose strength is a closed-form function of one dimensionless number, kappa;. Here we ask when this coupling destabilizes the gamma oscillator. The friction on gamma is negative during part of every theta cycle, yet gamma stays bounded: as long as it keeps oscillating, the energy gained while theta rises is returned while theta falls, and Liouville' sformula fixes the growth over a theta cycle at the baseline decay, whatever the coupling. Instability arises only in rare large theta cycles in which the friction exceeds critical damping, so that gamma stops oscillating and the gain is no longer returned. The typical trajectory becomes unstable when such cycles, about one in a hundred, outweigh the decay in all the others. This gives a boundary g* {sigma}x = 10, where {sigma}x is the typical theta amplitude set by the fluctuation dissipation theorem; the prediction agrees with a direct Lyapunov scan to within 6% for damping ratios from 0.0005 to 0.0055. The distance to the boundary is set by the same number kappa that sets the PAC strength, so that stronger PAC means closer proximity to instability. The mean-square boundary lies far lower but is set by events of negligible probability. Stimulating theta at or below its own frequency raises gamma energy and PAC and can drive giant gamma bursts or divergence, but no self-sustained activity, suggesting that a transition to seizure requires memory.

items.title: The creatine transporter SLC6A8 is an immune pressure-exposed metabolic vulnerability in acute myeloid leukemia
items.blurb: Chemotherapy imposes metabolic pressure that generates persisting tumor cell states, but whether these adaptations also shape immune evasion is poorly understood. Here, we identify creatine accumulation as a conserved feature of chemotherapy-persisting acute myeloid leukemia (AML) across mouse and human models. Stable-isotope tracing and genetic perturbation show that this is driven predominantly by SLC6A8-mediated creatine uptake rather than de novo synthesis. SLC6A8 was dispensable for AML proliferation and chemotherapy resistance but strongly promoted leukemia persistence under T cell pressure. This effect was independent of phosphocreatine generation and canonical energetic buffering. Instead, SLC6A8 deficiency increased cytokine-driven STAT1 signaling and chromatin remodeling, inducing the expression of antigen-presentation and co-stimulatory molecules, such as MHC-II, CD40, and CD80. Thus, creatine uptake via SLC6A8 is a non-canonical metabolic adaptation that restrains immune-driven remodeling and enables AML immune evasion. These findings link a therapy-induced metabolic adaptation to cytokine responsiveness and reveal SLC6A8 as a targetable vulnerability.

items.title: Phosphate selectivity in XPR1 is driven by direct multi-ion competition
items.blurb: Inorganic phosphate (Pi) is essential for numerous cellular processes, and its intracellular concentration must be tightly regulated. In mammals, phosphate efflux is mediated by the Xenotropic and Polytropic Retrovirus Receptor 1 (XPR1/SLC53A1), the only known mammalian Pi exporter. We and others have recently proposed that XPR1 functions like a Pi channel, with the protein preferentially conducting the H2PO4- species of Pi over HPO42-. While some studies suggest that XPR1 can conduct other anions, the molecular basis of XPR1 substrate selectivity remains unknown. Here, we use over 110 s of molecular dynamics simulations, together with free-energy calculations, to investigate substrate selectivity in XPR1. We show that H2PO4- (Pi1-) is preferentially conducted over HPO42- (Pi2-), and that Pi1- progressively outcompetes Cl- for occupancy of the transport pathway. Free-energy and ion-interaction analyses reveal that selectivity arises from two distinct mechanisms: favourable protein-Pi interactions and direct ion-ion interactions in the pore. This direct contact facilitates Pi1- displacement via the previously proposed knock-kiss-kick mechanism, whereas entry of Cl- is restricted due to the preference for water-mediated interactions. Simulations with additional anions show that XPR1 remains permissive to several monovalent species, including nitrate, bicarbonate and methanesulfonate, while poorly conducting the divalent anion sulfate. These findings suggest that XPR1 does not achieve phosphate selectivity through absolute exclusion of competing anions. Instead, preferential Pi transport emerges from substrate-specific interactions and competition between multiple ions within a relatively permissive permeation pathway, providing a molecular basis for substrate discrimination in XPR1.

items.title: A site-resolved post-translational modification framework for drug-response analysis
items.blurb: Post-translational modifications (PTMs) regulate protein activity and treatment-associated signalling, providing functional information that can connect drug-response estimates with candidate pharmacodynamic measurements. Assessing this information requires a framework that determines its contribution beyond fixed molecular features while retaining the identity of the modified sites underlying model predictions. We developed the PTM Biological Dynamics Layer (PTM-BDL), which integrates typed PTM states with protein sequence, structure-derived and drug chemical features to predict log-transformed half-maximal inhibitory concentration and resistance while providing site-level interpretation through integrated gradients. Retrospective evaluation used source-derived and propagated PTM profiles across biologically distinct BCR-ABL, HDAC/EP300 and EGFR/ERBB2 settings, yielding internal areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) between 0.785 and 0.946. Retraining demonstrated a consistent incremental contribution from PTM inputs in K562/CML, with a mean AUROC increase of 0.0268 and positive gains in all five folds, alongside more modest incremental gains in HeLa/HDAC and EGFR/ERBB2. Within K562/CML, CRKL Y207 and STAT5A Y694 retained the leading attribution ranks for their proteins across three seeds, while greater PTM attribution in dasatinib than in cytotoxic drug contexts identified a focused setting for pharmacodynamic investigation. These findings support context-dependent use of PTM information and connect predictive assessment with prioritisation of individual sites, providing a basis for targeted pharmacodynamic measurements and independent experimental validation.

items.title: MSGFLEX: An optimized end-to-end pipeline for proteomics and metaproteomics analysis built on MS-GF+ with a dedicated rescoring model XPECTRA
items.blurb: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics workflows often face competing demands between identification sensitivity, false discovery rate (FDR) control, and computational scalability, particularly for metaproteomic datasets that require searching large and complex sequence databases. Here, we present MSGFLEX, an integrated end-to-end workflow that combines database searching, machine-learning based rescoring, and peptide-to-protein quantitative inference. MSGFLEX integrates three components: SPARX handles raw file conversion, and MS-GF+ database searching; XPECTRA is a cross-validated XGBoost ensemble that rescores peptide-spectrum matches by combining ensemble predictions with MS-GF+ search evidence through noisy-OR fusion model.
