QUANTIX provides protein quantification through multiple protein rollup strategies. Across four benchmarking datasets, XPECTRA consistently increased peptide and protein identifications relative to Percolator, MS2Rescore, and MSBooster. On a human gut metaproteome dataset, XPECTRA achieved the largest effect size among all methods evaluated (Cohen's d = 0.95; p < 0.0005). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based analysis indicated that XPECTRA learned consistent relationships from spectral and physicochemical features. Database partitioning does not introduce detectable bias in peptide identification or FDR estimation, while QUANTIX's DWrollup provides the most accurate recovery of known protein abundance changes in a ground-truth spike-in benchmark. Together, these results establish MSGFLEX as a scalable and interpretable framework for mass-spectrometry based proteomics and metaproteomics.

items.title: The genetic basis of adaptation to continuous environmental gradients informs predictions about climate change responses
items.blurb: A central goal of evolutionary genetics is to determine how environmental pressures maintain adaptive genetic variation, and evaluate how this variation is encoded in the genome. We leveraged two powerful approaches to identify genomic regions associated with climatic adaptation, test the genetic basis of climatic adaptation, and predict genomic responses to novel climates: genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of climate niche parameters derived from demographic models and genome-environment associations (GEA) of climatic factors with 2,737,409 loci. The GWAS found 319 unique single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with climate niche parameters derived from demographic models using multi-year manipulative field experiments with Boechera stricta. The GEA detected 154 unique SNPs linked to climatic variation, with only one SNP found in both approaches. Local adaptation via adult survival arose primarily through conditional neutrality, as local alleles outperformed foreign alleles at only one end of the climatic gradient, rather than genetic trade-offs. Candidate genes near these loci were implicated in stress responses. Contrary to expectations, increasing temperatures and accelerating snowmelt timings did not augment the absolute fitness of low elevation genotypes. We found non-linear fitness functions for seedling recruitment at multiple SNPs detected via GWAS, with both conditional neutrality and genetic trade-offs evident in different portions of the climatic gradient. Local maladaptation arose exclusively in GEA SNPs. Our analyses revealed that the hot and dry conditions projected under climate change may rapidly exceed the tolerance of this species. However, we identified 47 SNPs at which evolutionary rescue or assisted migration could ameliorate the reduction in fitness under climate change.

items.title: Comprehensive identification of bacterial and archaeal habitat associations using IndicPiper
items.blurb: Taxa that are prevalent and abundant in a particular habitat more so than other habitats can be considered indicators of that habitat. In addition to providing basic natural history information, indicator taxa can be used to verify metadata assignments in large public databases, identify potential contamination, and assess contributions of different source populations to a sink population. Despite these potential applications, a comprehensive database of microbial indicator taxa for major habitats of interest does not yet exist. Here we present IndicPiper, a database and methodology that uses the Sandpiper database combined with indicator taxa analysis to identify the habitat associations of bacterial and archaeal genera. IndicPiper includes a clearly defined methodology and set of functions such that any user with a list of habitats of interest could run the functions and generate their own database. IndicPiper uses the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) for taxonomy, and the provided database or custom databases can be used to analyze any prokaryotic sample-by-taxa abundance table, including those from shotgun metagenomic and 16S rRNA marker gene sequencing. After presenting the methodology and results, we then present three applications of IndicPiper on actual modern and ancient DNA sequencing datasets. We used IndicPiper to assess the contribution of different source habitats to Lake Tjornin sediments in Iceland over the past 2000 years, to paired indoor and outdoor dust samples from homes across the U.S, and to freshwater samples across the Willamette River watershed in Oregon, USA.

items.title: Antibody-Fcγ receptor-driven NOX2 activation during phagocytosis of tumor cells is suppressed by CD47, preventing CD8 T cell engagement and immunotherapeutic responses.
items.blurb: Antibody-dependent cellular phagocytosis (ADCP) contributes to the elimination of antibody-opsonized tumor cells and engagement of adaptive immunity. This process is inhibited by tumor-cell overexpression of CD47. Here, genome-wide CRISPR screens in macrophages identified the NADPH oxidase (NOX2 complex) and the CD47 receptor, SIRP, as regulators of phagosome acidification. Target-cell CD47 suppressed NOX2 generation of reactive oxygen species at antibody densities that support ADCP, revealing distinct CD47-dependent thresholds for ADCP and oxidant generation. CD47 removal from the target cell delayed phagosome acidification in wild-type macrophages, but not in NOX2-deficient macrophages. Consistent with a role for this pathway in antitumor immunity, tumor-opsonizing anti-Tyrp1 therapy allowed clearance of CD47-deficient B16F10 melanoma tumors in approximately 36% of wild-type mice but failed in NOX2-deficient mice. Tumor clearance required CD8 T cells and IFN{gamma}, but perforin was dispensable. CD4 T cell depletion markedly improved tumor clearance. These findings suggest a noncanonical role for CD8 T cells in supporting ADCP-mediated tumor control. Combining anti-Tyrp1 with a mouse-serum-albumin-IL-2 fusion (MSA-IL-2) or PD-1 blockade enabled superior clearance of CD47-deficient tumors in NOX2-deficient mice, but not wild-type mice. Rechallenge experiments distinguished primary tumor clearance from durable immunity, whereby NOX2-deficient mice treated with anti-Tyrp1 and PD-1 blockade lacked rechallenge protection despite high initial cure rates. Conversely, the addition of MSA-IL-2 supported durable protection in both wild-type and NOX2-deficient mice. These results indicate that tumor CD47 functions beyond a "don't-eat-me" signal by controlling NOX2 activity to positively and negatively regulate CD 8 T cell function. Significance CD47-SIRP suppresses NOX2 activation, regulating a critical feedback loop between ADCP and CD8 T cell activation during tumor-opsonizing antibody therapy, suggesting new strategies for cancer immunotherapy targeting tumor surface antigens.

items.title: Immunometabolic IRG1-NLRC5 Axis Controls Inflammatory Cell Death
items.blurb: Innate immunity is the first defense against pathogens, sterile injury, and homeostatic perturbations. One key mechanism used by the innate immune system for host defense is inflammatory cell death, PANoptosis, which eliminates infected or damaged cells and releases cytokines and other danger signals that can further propagate the immune response. Given these inflammatory functions, PANoptosis must be tightly regulated to prevent excess inflammation and pathology. Cellular metabolism is a key regulator of innate immunity, yet how metabolic reprogramming regulates innate immune signaling to control cell death, inflammation, and disease remains poorly understood. Here, we identify the immune-responsive gene 1 (IRG1)-itaconate axis as a critical regulator of PANoptosis. Innate immune triggers robustly induced IRG1 expression, leading to itaconate accumulation and driving IRG1-dependent inflammatory cell death. Mechanistically, glutaminolysis fueled IRG1-dependent itaconate synthesis, and inhibition of glutamine metabolism reduced itaconate accumulation and blocked PANoptosis. Furthermore, NAD depletion, a known inducer of NLRC5-mediated PANoptosis that has been connected to hemolytic, infectious, and inflammatory conditions, acted upstream inducing IRG1 expression and promoting NLRC5-PANoptosome assembly. Together, these findings highlight IRG1 as a metabolic node linking innate immunity to PANoptosis, identifying IRG1 as a potential therapeutic target in hemolytic and inflammatory diseases.

items.title: Early Life Shift in Fear Extinction is Driven by Prefrontal-Amygdala Engagement
items.blurb: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) displays a delayed maturation long hypothesized to guide developmental changes in threat processing. Nevertheless, the mechanism by which ontogenetic changes in mPFC function guide the developmental emergence of behavior is unclear. Early life marks a shift between a permanent extinction phenotype typical of juveniles, toward the standard, more transient extinction seen in adult rodents. This shift coincides with developmental changes in mPFC-amygdala connectivity, a pathway necessary for extinction processing in adults. Here we used optogenetics and slice electrophysiology to show that, in contrast to adult animals, juvenile mice displaying permanent extinction fail to engage the mPFC-amygdala pathway at the synaptic, cell activity or behavioral levels. Consistent with a requirement of this pathway for the developmental transition in extinction types, optic potentiation of the mPFC-amygdala pathway accelerates the onset of adult extinction. Our findings show that the developmental onboarding of the mPFC-amygdala pathway drives a shift in extinction processing toward increased fear reemergence that persists throughout adulthood.

items.title: Harmonizing resting-state functional MRI data to increase sample size and to classify tinnitus brain connectivity
items.blurb: Tinnitus, or ringing in the ears, is a hearing disorder that affects approximately 15% of human adults globally. The neuroscientific understanding of this subjective disorder is limited at present, partly due to a lack of sufficient neuroimaging data to compensate for the heterogeneity in the disorder; neural data acquisition is often impeded by low patient counts and doubled costs against scanning ample controls. However, with the increase in data sharing practices, data scarcity can be overcome with harmonization methods if scans from independent sites and studies are pooled successfully. To achieve data harmonization for limited data from a tinnitus neuroimaging study, we merged a modest fMRI dataset acquired in our lab (n=35) with age- and gender-matched samples from another large dataset, the Lifespan Human Connectome Project Aging (n=377). We measured functional connectivity (FC) between brain regions based on resting-state fMRI session scans, and used deep learning architecture to systematically combine individual FCs across the datasets. We assembled and trained neural network modules to purge dataset-identifying information from FC maps, and retained patterns that can characterize tinnitus-related FC. Hallmark artifactual information of the datasets was significantly reduced while reconstructing resting state FC data. Relevant relationships in brain connectivity that discern the condition of tinnitus from controls were well-preserved in the reconstructed resting state FC data. In agreement with existing literature on brain networks of tinnitus, connectivity related to default mode, ventral attention and frontoparietal control networks were identified to be crucial for distinguishing the condition, as masking these networks connections severely impacted downstream classification prediction on reconstructed FC. The data harmonization model was successful in merging FC matrices from independently acquired fMRI datasets, without losing out on meaningful functional connectivity patterns of interest for the neuropsychological disorder of tinnitus. Our findings demonstrate the potential of data harmonization by integrating independently acquired datasets on healthy controls to overcome neuroimaging data scarcity while preserving disorder-relevant neural signatures, advancing research on understudied neurological disorders.

items.title: BrainRoute integrates machine learning prediction with community-driven verification of blood-brain barrier permeability
items.blurb: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) is a highly selective barrier that restricts the entry of many therapeutic agents into the brain. The lack of efficient methods for BBB permeability research and data management remains a significant challenge for central nervous system drug-development pipelines. Although BBB permeability data are available from multiple open sources, few platforms integrate these datasets with molecular exploration, predictive tools, and a structured process for community-supported data verification. Here, we present BrainRoute, an open platform for BBB molecular data collection, exploration, prediction, and community-supported verification. BrainRoute provides searchable and filterable molecular records, physicochemical and structural information, source-linked data, single-molecule and batch prediction, and a structured workflow through which users can submit additional evidence for review. The prediction tool model-development cohort contained 7,888 unique molecules, including 5,424 BBB+ and 2,464 BBB- molecules. Six machine-learning classifiers were evaluated using PaDEL descriptors, Morgan fingerprints, frozen ChemBERTa embeddings, and combined feature representations. The three selected models were integrated into the platform as a probability-averaged ensemble. The primary five-fold scaffold-grouped analysis achieved a best mean balanced accuracy of 0.783 {+/-} 0.026. On an independent external set containing 410 non-overlapping molecules, the deployed ensemble achieved a balanced accuracy of 0.659 (95% CI 0.600 - 0.712) and an AUPRC of 0.670 (95% CI 0.583 - 0.752). BrainRoute serves as a platform for exploring BBB-related molecular data and computational predictions while supporting the continued growth and verification of the underlying dataset. BrainRoute is freely accessible online (https://github.com/omicscodeathon/brainroutedb).

items.title: When spike sorting matters: single-neuron identity in the quantification of neural circuits
items.blurb: Multiunit threshold crossings support high-performance brain-computer interfaces and preserve the low-dimensional trajectories that summarize population dynamics, raising the question of when spike sorting is still necessary. Using previously published recordings from four rhesus monkeys, we analyzed areas 3b and 1 of primary somatosensory cortex and ventral premotor cortex during a bimodal detection task, and ventral premotor cortex during an interval comparison task. From the same spikes, we built three representations: putative single units obtained with nonlinear sorting (UMAP and HDBSCAN), intermingled units obtained with linear sorting, and unsorted multiunit activity. Nonlinear sorting resolved up to three times more units than multiunit activity. In area 1, mixing discarded the periodicity information carried by phase-locked neurons, lengthened intrinsic timescales by about 40%, increased trial-to-trial variability, and raised neurometric detection thresholds by 33%. In premotor cortex, mixing reduced the task-related information recovered from the population and hid significant dimensions of its dynamics. After geometric alignment, the overall shape of population trajectories was nearly identical across representations, but distances between population states were distorted, and the approximately linear representation of interval duration saturated for longer intervals. Multiunit activity is therefore sufficient for analyses that rely on the dominant, shared structure of population activity, such as decoding, whereas analyses of single-neuron coding, variability, timescales, dimensionality, and parametric representations often require spike sorting.

items.title: PolyMorph3D: A flexible MATLAB-based tool for quantifying microglia morphology and multi-colocalization in three dimensions
items.blurb: As the principle immune cell of the central nervous system (CNS), microglia have been extensively studied throughout development and in a wide range of disease states. Of special focus have been their morphological features such as branching complexity, physical cell-cell interactions with surroundings, and gene expression readouts relating to phagocytosis and cytokine signaling. Each of these domains offers a window onto microglia function, and high-resolution confocal microscopy has long been a workhorse technique to visualize all three. A comprehensive view of microglia function requires both high-fidelity quantification with 3D resolution and colocalization of microglia with functional proteins such as those related to phagocytosis and with nearby structures such as synapses. Accordingly, a number of analytical tools have been developed to measure these features. However, existing open-source options lack either colocalization or 3D capability, while commercial solutions can be costly. Here, we sought to develop an open-source solution that addresses each of these limitations. PolyMorph3D is a MATLAB-based program capable of yielding individual cell-level data of microglia morphology and overlap with up to 4 other sources, all in 3D. The pipeline can be used effectively in mouse tissue and in human postmortem brain, thereby offering a flexible, low cost, and high-fidelity solution for the analysis of microglial morphology and function.

items.title: Trial history and model-derived reward prediction errors in mousevisual decisions
items.blurb: A reward prediction error (RPE) estimated from an animal's behavior can predict its next choice. Part of this predictive value may come from information about earlier trials that a choice model could also use directly. We asked whether a model-derived RPE improves choice prediction beyond the observable history of stimuli, choices, and rewards. We analyzed 275,292 trials from 107 mice performing the International Brain Laboratory visual decision task and evaluated the main choice models on sessions that were not used for fitting. Recent choices strongly improved prediction. An RPE based on a stimulus-dependent reward expectation added a small gain beyond the preceding choice and reward, and this gain fell to near zero once the model included the preceding stimulus. When the model also summarized choices and rewards over several earlier trials, an RPE trace with the same retention parameter as the history traces did not reliably improve prediction. In simulated agents with known decision rules, a simplified version of this comparison detected an RPE-based learning rule in which choices depended on accumulated prediction errors, and did not improve prediction for an agent that used trial history directly. In mice, the state-dependent RPE and its trace added little predictive information beyond observable trial history, which limits what choice prediction alone can reveal about prediction-error learning.

items.title: HCM-mutation G716R in β-myosin alters contractile function and responsiveness to mavacamten of human ventricular myofibrils
items.blurb: Effects of the hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) associated mutation Gly716Arg in {beta}-myosin at the sarcomeric level are unresolved. To further understand HCM-pathomechanisms in relation to modern treatment, we investigated the effect of this mutation in subcellular myofibrils isolated from HCM-patient myocardium compared to myofibrils from healthy donor hearts and tested how mavacamten influences force-related parameters. Mavacamten is a state-of-the-art myosin inhibitor aimed to treat ventricular hypercontractility of symptomatic HCM patients. Compared with donor myofibrils, patient myofibrils developed similar isometric forces, while kinetics of maximum force generation and particularly of relaxation were slower. Relaxation impairment was exacerbated when patient myofibrils were incompletely relaxed to mimic residual diastolic calcium levels. Inhibitory effects of mavacamten were dependent on force activation level and significantly less efficient in patient myofibrils. While the drug accelerated full relaxation of donor myofibrils, the slowing down effect of the mutation was not reversed by the drug in patient myofibrils. At partial relaxation, impairment was further aggravated by mavacamten in patient myofibrils. This study suggests that HCM-associated mutation G716R in {beta}-myosin does not evoke gain-of-function in human left ventricular myofibrils, and impaired relaxation could not be rescued by mavacamten. Our findings suggest that HCM-associated mutations may modulate myofibrillar sensitivity to mavacamten, providing a potential mechanistic explanation for differences in treatment response. Studies such as the present one highlight the importance of mutation-dependent sarcomeric properties in understanding variability in responses to myosin modulators and potentially informing more individualized treatment strategies.

items.title: Behavioral Plasticity and Dispersal of Free Swimming Coral Larvae via Vertical Tracking Microscopy
items.blurb: Coral larvae disperse and seek suitable sites for settlement while undergoing rapid development, making this period central to reef connectivity, recruitment, and recovery. Yet how the accompanying changes in larval morphology, ciliary activity, and swimming behavior shape dispersal remains poorly understood. Here, using vertical tracking microscopy, we follow individual Acropora millepora larvae over hundreds of body lengths at successive developmental stages while resolving body morphology. We show a developmental progression from buoyant rise to upward- and downward-directed gravitactic swimming, followed by weaker gravitactic alignment at later stages, accompanied by body elongation and increasingly structured ciliary flows. Integrating these kinematics into a minimal, data-driven model, we separate buoyant drift from active swimming and estimate the propulsion costs of vertical migration and lateral spreading. Buoyancy supports early ascent without propulsion expenditure, while the model predicts lower costs of descent and lateral spreading at late developmental stages. Simulations in fluctuating flow, assuming no flow sensing, predict that directed swimming weakens when flow-induced rotation acts on timescales comparable to intrinsic heading relaxation. Together, these results reveal how development reorganizes the physical drivers of larval motion in ways that may support the transition from dispersal to settlement, providing a basis for incorporating developmental changes in swimming into models of coral larval dispersal.

items.title: 'PAC-MAN' capsules that gobble up particles in turbulent water show promise for filtration and drug delivery
items.blurb: Scientists have created hollow capsules with single openings that can selectively filter particles thanks to the turbulence in surrounding waters—at times, ingesting particles like PAC-MAN eating up dots.

items.title: Britain should treat healthy seas as essential infrastructure, say scientists
items.blurb: Researchers are calling for lasting investment in healthy seas to support food security, protect coastlines and strengthen economic resilience.

items.title: The secret of 'strange metals' may lie in quantum statistics, not collisions
items.blurb: In an ordinary metal, electrons behave like well-defined particles that occasionally bump into imperfections or vibrations of the crystal. Many materials with strong electron–electron interactions, including the copper-oxide (cuprate) superconductors, break these rules. In these "strange metals," electrical resistance rises in a straight line with temperature over a very wide range. Electrons seem to lose their momentum at the fastest rate quantum mechanics allows, the so-called Planckian limit. What causes this is still an open question.

items.title: Euclid's hunt for strong gravitational lenses is off to a strong start
items.blurb: If dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

items.title: Staying alive in marsh muck: The tiny 'snorkels' cattails grow manipulate soil chemistry
items.blurb: Cattails are a familiar sight in wetlands, where they thrive in both brackish and freshwater marshes. But surviving in waterlogged soil presents a challenge; their roots need oxygen in an environment where very little is available.

items.title: Dual-purpose polymer dots could combine bioimaging and light-triggered cell death in one material
items.blurb: A research team led by professor Youhei Takeda at the University of Osaka, in collaboration with professor Zachary M. Hudson at the University of British Columbia (UBC) in Canada, has developed a polymer material that combines fluorescent cell imaging with the potential to kill cancer cells when activated by light. The material could offer a simpler approach to developing "nanotheranostic" technologies, which bring disease imaging and treatment together in a single platform.

items.title: Individual meerkats are ace solo navigators
items.blurb: After meerkats emerge each morning from their burrow to warm in the early sun, there's one thing on their collective mind, and that's to find food. They navigate communally as they head off, working slowly along their route before returning home swiftly at the end of the day. But although the tight-knit band navigates as one, some members of the clan could be more experienced after roaming solo, shaping the community's maneuvers.

items.title: How microbes make drug-like chemicals without damaging themselves
items.blurb: University of Michigan researchers have discovered a mechanism that enables microscopic organisms like bacteria and fungi to produce drug-like molecules—compounds that can fight infections or kill cancer cells—without damaging themselves.

items.title: ESA's Hera probe uses 'superhuman' vision to inspect NASA's asteroid crash site
items.blurb: Around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour (13,700 miles per hour). However, we still don't know just how much of a success it actually was—DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up.

items.title: If tiny 'primordial' black holes exist, here's how we might find them
items.blurb: Scientists have hypothesized that, in the fraction of a second following the Big Bang, minute black holes may have been forged within tiny, dense pockets that collapsed under their own gravity. If these primordial black holes are ever found, they could represent a significant component of dark matter—the invisible substance that makes up most of the universe's matter.

items.title: The snake with a built-in egg peeler
items.blurb: Dr. Arthur Tiutenko from FAU and colleagues from LMU München and the South African National Museum in Bloemfontein discovered a new species of snake in the Harenna Forest, on the southern slopes of Ethiopia's Bale Mountains: Dasypeltis albigularis, or the white-throated egg-eater. "Three other new species in this genus are still waiting in line," the zoologist adds.

items.title: How a tiny chemical mark on a protein can be placed to double gene activity
items.blurb: Tiny chemical marks on histones—the proteins that package our DNA—can profoundly influence gene activity without changing the underlying DNA sequence. One such mark, known as histone acetylation, plays a crucial role in regulating gene expression and is frequently disrupted in diseases such as cancer. Researchers, however, wondered how the enzymes responsible for adding these marks know exactly where to place them.

items.title: Lonely shoppers demonstrate less compassion in their purchases than others, study shows
items.blurb: Chronically lonely people are less likely to buy products that benefit others, such as fair-trade or child-labor-free goods, according to a new study by researchers at Concordia and the University of the Fraser Valley. The team ran four studies involving more than 1,400 participants across North America. Each person completed a standard loneliness questionnaire, then chose between ordinary products and versions that cost 15% to 20% more but carried an ethical or environmental label. Items included toothpaste, chocolate bars, jackets and backpacks.

items.title: Light-activated nanoparticles may help treat head and neck cancer
items.blurb: For patients with head and neck cancer, treatment can come at a high cost to their quality of life, affecting their ability to speak, swallow and even breathe due to invasive procedures. Now, Penn State researchers have developed a light-activated nanoparticle system with the long-term goal of shrinking tumors while limiting exposure to healthy tissue and improving patients' quality of life after cancer treatment. Penn State has licensed the technology to Illuminate Therapeutics, which is advancing its preclinical development.

items.title: Ethiopian volcano's mysterious methane outburst may have a culprit—magma that never erupted
items.blurb: Experts were puzzled when satellite observations showed a volcano in Ethiopia emitting huge quantities of methane despite not erupting, but a team of researchers led by the University of Bristol believe they have discovered why this happened—and their findings could have implications for historical climate change research.

items.title: Ahead of Giving Tuesday, study finds charitable giving often misses communities with greatest need
items.blurb: As Giving Tuesday approaches, a recent study led by a University of Massachusetts Amherst public policy researcher finds that communities with greater economic disadvantage typically see less private charitable giving—despite having greater needs in many cases.

items.title: Gene variant gives male malaria mosquitoes a mating edge in the heat
items.blurb: Mosquitoes play a major role in spreading malaria, and understanding how they adapt to climate change is important for improving malaria prevention and control.

items.title: Cichlid sibling rivalry: Young fish fight more in some species than others
items.blurb: Though we may fight with our siblings sometimes, for most people a sibling is a constant companion throughout childhood and often for one's entire life. Yet this is not always the case in the animal kingdom: in some species, siblings engage in serious fights that can even escalate to fratricide. They may be genetically related, but must also compete for limited resources.

items.title: Rethinking the 'girls are worse with money' myth
items.blurb: New research led by Dr. Stephen Agnew from Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury's (UC) Department of Economics and Finance is challenging one of the most persistent assumptions in education and everyday culture: that teenage girls are less financially literate than boys.

items.title: Remote jobs diminish hiring bias against mothers
items.blurb: The "motherhood penalty"—a workplace bias that assumes mothers are less committed to their careers, resulting in fewer opportunities, lower pay and slower advancement—could be reduced by shifting jobs from in-person to remote, according to new research by Claire Daviss, assistant professor of organizational behavior at the ILR School.

items.title: Optical DNA mapping assembles yeast genomes at chromosome scale
items.blurb: Large, complex genomes remain difficult to characterize accurately, even with modern DNA sequencing. Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology have now extended an optical genome mapping approach, previously demonstrated for bacterial genomes, to more complex eukaryotic genomes. Using two yeast species, they generated optical maps covering entire chromosomes, including large repetitive regions that are particularly difficult to reconstruct.

items.title: How Future Lunar Colonists Can Farm Potatoes on the Moon
items.blurb: A new study discovered a recipe for success

items.title: How Our Eyes Betray Us When We Lie
items.blurb: Subtle shifts in gaze can signal we’re hiding something

items.title: Tiny, threadlike connections act as ‘skyways’ between cells
items.blurb: When a young researcher suggested cells trade resources through microscopic pipelines, many colleagues refused to believe it. Two decades later, these tunneling nanotubes are being studied for roles in cancer and other diseases.

items.title: Secrets of a superfruit: The açaí genome gets decoded
items.blurb: Investigating the little fruit’s DNA is already revealing clues to its rich color and may help define distinct terroirs for this emblem of Brazil’s bioeconomy

items.title: A cytoskeletal toggle switch controls amnion architecture and fate
items.blurb: Binary cellular decisions are generally attributed to gene regulatory networks, with cytoskeletal-driven shape changes often treated as an output. Yet, whether the cytoskeleton can itself implement switch-like logic to drive abrupt morphological transitions remains unknown. In the primate amniotic sac, the extraembryonic amnion derives directly from the columnar epiblast and abruptly flattens into a squamous epithelium to form a highly asymmetric cavity. Here, we identify a cytoskeletal switch driving this developmental bifurcation in human gastrula models. Mutual inhibition between actomyosin and keratin networks generates two mechanical attractors: amnion cells flip into a keratin-rich, squamous shape, while the epiblast remains myosin-rich and columnar. Ectopic activation of YAP1-TEAD signaling triggers the myosin-keratin switch without inducing amnion specification, establishing that the switch is not simply a consequence of fate changes. Conversely, preventing the switch disrupts amnion specification, showing that this shape bifurcation gates lineage commitment. Single-cell transcriptomics across cytoskeletal perturbations revealed a transcriptional signature for the toggle switch, which is recapitulated in vivo in the human and marmoset amnion. Together, our findings show that the cytoskeleton acts not only as an effector of tissue shape but as a decision-making module, implementing the same toggle switch logic as gene regulatory networks to drive morphological bifurcations.

items.title: Modelling vortex interactions reveals distinct patterns of brain reconfiguration following psilocybin and escitalopram
items.blurb: Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, yet how interventions reorganise brain dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how psilocybin and escitalopram reshape brain dynamics in depression using pre- and post-treatment resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) from a double-blind randomised controlled trial (NCT03429075). We compared two whole-brain modelling approaches: conventional signal-space modelling describing interactions between regional brain signals, and vortex-space modelling capturing interactions between evolving patterns of local synchronisation. This represents the first application of vortex-space modelling to a psychiatric disorder. Vortex space was more sensitive than signal space in most analyses, including distinguishing treatment-related brain states, relating baseline connectivity to clinical improvement and predicting response to escitalopram. Our results further revealed distinct patterns of reorganisation following the two interventions. Psilocybin produced widespread increases in vortex-space effective connectivity and reduced network modularity, whereas escitalopram showed no comparable changes. Despite these differences, greater increases in brain turbulence (i.e., spatiotemporal variability in local synchronisation) were associated with greater symptom reduction in both treatments, with a significant post-treatment increase in responders. These findings suggest that psilocybin and escitalopram may reorganise brain dynamics in markedly different ways and yet share dynamical features associated with clinical improvement. Overall, vortex-space modelling offers a promising framework for characterising brain dynamics in depression and its successful treatment.

items.title: Data-Driven Decomposition of Precisely Aligned Fiber-Orientation-Preserving Probabilistic Tractography Connectomes with Non-Negative Matrix Factorization
items.blurb: The major goals of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) were to characterize the structural and functional connectivity of the human brain. Although there has been tremendous work done for functional connectivity, including application of a variety of data driven decomposition approaches, structural connectivity from the HCP has seen less attention. This work presents a collection of methodological advances that, in combination, enable similar approaches to be applied to diffusion tractography data. Here, we use multi-modal non-linear volumetric alignment with FSL's MultiMOdal Registration Framework (MMORF) to precisely align white matter tracts and globular gray matter nuclei, use the White matter Hierarchical Modelling (WHIM) method to align voxel-wise fiber orientations, enable efficient GPU-accelerated computation and storage of full resolution probabilistic gray matter x white matter x fiber sparse tractography matrices in precise alignment across individuals using the aforementioned MMORF and WHIM alignments together with areal-feature-based cortical surface registration. These tractography dense connectomes can be averaged across individuals and sparse, computationally efficient non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) can be applied to perform data-driven decompositions into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories. The primary outputs of this effort to date are 1) A set of HCP software pipelines enabling such analyses, 2) A new unbiased HCP-derived volumetric standard space that is representative of the young adult brain and follows ACPC orientation conventions across individuals. 3) Reproducible NMF decompositions of HCP young adult tractography data into white matter tracts and gray matter projection territories, which could be projected using non-negative dual regression back to individuals. These data represent a starting point for a new generation of data-driven atlasing efforts for human white matter, and these methods can be applied to study the white matter in development, aging, and brain diseases.

items.title: ASTEROID, A Validated Annotated Dataset of Analytical Decisions in Graph Theory Based fMRI
items.blurb: Graph theory-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies use complex analytical pipelines, but methodological decisions are often reported in unstructured text, limiting systematic comparison and the design of multiverse analyses. Here, we describe ASTEROID, a structured annotation dataset derived from 156 graph theory-based human fMRI study publications. Its schema contains 125 labels, comprising 61 methodological labels and 64 labels for study characteristics and experimental design. An LLM-assisted workflow generated initial annotations, which underwent automated quality-control checks and expert human review. The dataset captures preprocessing, functional connectivity, and graph-analysis decisions. Within these categories, steps and their sequence, software, algorithms, parameters, and supporting text spans are included where available. This accompanying paper provides prompt specifications, processing scripts, and documentation, and describes an interactive viewer that supports exploration of the annotation schema and the study records. ASTEROID enables comparison of reported analytical choices, the informed design of multiverse-based robustness analysis and supports the development and evaluation of automated methodological information-extraction tools and educational resources for fMRI data analysis.

items.title: Comparative Analysis of Orthologous ANK-NLR-WRKY Proteins in Wheat Species: Evolutionary Divergence and Structural Characteristics
items.blurb: The plant nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptors are known to play a crucial role in plant host defence against a variety of biotic stresses. Several NLR proteins contain integrated domains (NLR-ID) like ankyrin (ANK) and WRKY transcription factor domains and are important evolutionary adaptations in plant immunity. They are responsible for the perception of effector molecules from invading pathogens and pests and subsequent activation of plant immune responses. However, the functional roles these ANK-NLR-WRKY proteins play in wheat (Triticum aestivum) against various pathogens and pests remain poorly understood. Computational tools employed for comparative sequence and phylogenetic analyses revealed that TaAdnr1 is highly conserved across diploid (T. urartu), tetraploid (T. dicoccoides), and hexaploid (T. aestivum) wheat species, including its well characterised orthologue YrU1 from T. urartu. Three-dimensional (3D) protein structural modelling using AlphaFold2 supported strong conservation in the multiple domains of these NLR orthologues, more specifically within the integrated WRKY domain. This conservation may suggest a strong evolutionary maintenance of TaADNR1. Furthermore, this may also suggest TaADNR1 reflects specificity in effector recognition and regulation. Therefore, the integration of functional genomics studies, sequence analysis, evolutionary analysis and structural modelling possesses the potential to provide new insights into the pleiotropic roles of integrated domain NLRs in wheat.

items.title: Evaluation of sources of variability in a TEER (trans-epithelial/endothelial electrical resistance) system
items.blurb: Trans-epithelial/endothelial electrical resistance (TEER) measurements are a key nondestructive measurement of the barrier integrity of cells grown on inserts. To support the use of TEER measurements in bioassays, we have evaluated the sources of variability in a case study involving a chamber-based TEER system to assess a gut co-culture model. Data from 23 separate experiments, each lasting 22 d, were evaluated. Multiple lines of evidence suggested minimal variability within a run, a period during which several plates were analyzed sequentially. In contrast, run-to-run variability was substantially larger, even when two runs were performed several hours apart on the same day. Bayesian analysis of both KCl and blank insert data revealed that run-to-run variability was among the largest sources of variability, with relative uncertainty values of 3 % to 6 % of the mean value. Correlational analysis investigated whether deviations of KCl or blank insert TEER values within a run compared to long-term median values were correlated with deviations of the biculture gut model values within that same run from their long-term median values. Unexpectedly, the KCl values were not correlated, while the blank insert values had a weak correlation. We also evaluated the information gained from different control measurements. The findings from this study can influence how statistical analyses are performed on TEER results and can inform the design of robust TEER methods. For example, the approaches described here can be used to characterize variability within and among runs in TEER measurements for other methods.

items.title: Bioresorbable permanent-magnet beacons for tracking internal biomechanics during free movement
items.blurb: Perioperative complications represent a global health burden that can be reduced through timely interventions guided by continuous physiological monitoring. Bioresorbable sensors excel through natural degradation without subsequent surgical extraction, but motion artefacts disrupt their accurate measurement. We synthesize bioresorbable permanent-magnet nanocomposites from aligned iron nanowires as implantable beacons. These beacons intrinsically generate magnetic fields responsive to biomechanical changes, thereby enabling wireless and chipless monitoring. An artificial-intelligence-enhanced wearable magnetic-field camera decodes these spatial maps into calibrated values that tolerate vigorous movement. The system achieves a displacement-equivalent mean absolute error of 2.74 m. Experiments in rat models demonstrate intracranial pressure tracking with clinical-grade accuracy during vigorous activities, and longitudinal monitoring of intracranial hypertension associated with ischaemic stroke during natural behaviours.

items.title: Continuous karyotypic and cryptic structural fluctuations drive acral melanoma evolution
items.blurb: Reliable chromosome segregation during mitosis is essential for high-fidelity mammalian cell division. Even human cancers burdened by whole genome duplication and aneuploidy generally retain sufficiently stable segregation to produce clonal populations of progeny. Cancer genomes are accordingly understood to evolve in punctuated bursts, in which catastrophic rearrangement is followed by clonal expansion of a stabilized karyotype. However, bulk genomic sequencing, the workhorse of cancer genetics for the past two decades, cannot resolve structural variability within tumor subpopulations. Here we identify a subset of cancers that exhibit continuous ultra-low fidelity chromosomal segregation, with single tumors harboring individual cells whose metaphase chromosome counts ranged from 25 to over 200. This remarkable phenotype is recurrent in multiple cancer types and most common in acral melanoma, where it is associated with dicentric chromosomes, translocations, and complex structural variants. Single-cell whole genome sequencing revealed ongoing structural variation and the genomic signature of microhomology-mediated break-induced replication (MMBIR), a backup DNA repair pathway that triggers chromoanasynthesis. These genomes therefore do not pass through isolated catastrophic events and settle into stable lineages but rather undergo continuous evolution of chromosome number and structure across generations, resulting in extreme intratumoral heterogeneity and a shifting repertoire of gene fusions. We anticipate these findings will serve as a starting point for classifying tumors by ongoing karyotypic and structural fluctuation and for testing whether this state confers selective dependence on backup repair pathways.

items.title: How gradual evolution, fitness landscapes, and trait associations shape mutation rates in large populations
items.blurb: Mutation rates are evolvable traits that respond to selection partly through the associations of modifier alleles with other variants affecting individual fitness. Yet, these variants can be subject to various selective regimes, whose respective role in shaping the evolution of mutation rates remains incompletely understood. To clarify the links between the fitness landscape and selection on mutation rates, we analyse a multi-locus continuum-of-alleles model where traits can affect both individual fitness and the mutation rates expressed across loci. We obtain a closed hierarchical system of moments describing the change in the distribution of traits, and thus in mutation rates, under small trait variation. We find that variation in mutation rates across individuals builds skew in the trait distribution, which plays a key role in the evolution of mutation rates; to track such asymmetries, we go beyond classical normal closure and adapt a cumulant-neglect method. We show that positive mutation rates are favoured by indirect selection out of evolutionary equilibrium (under directional, fluctuating or diversifying selection) and selected against at equilibrium (under homogenising selection). We illustrate these cases with a two-trait model, which we also study using individual-based simulations to evaluate the robustness of our deterministic results to genetic drift. Beyond these examples, our results classify the selective mechanisms acting on mutation rates and rank their importance according to the local shape of the fitness landscape and the variational properties of the population. This provides an account of the different ways selection can act on transmission fidelity in large populations.

items.title: The virome of New Zealand fur seals reveals novel viral diversity and evidence of continued Canine distemper virus circulation
items.blurb: Canine distemper virus (CDV) has recently been detected in New Zealand fur seals (Arctocephalus forsteri), including retrospective samples from 2020 and outbreaks associated with substantial mortality in late 2024 and 2025. However, the geographic distribution of CDV and the broader viral diversity harboured by New Zealand fur seals remain poorly understood. Characterising the fur seal virome can provide insights into viral diversity, dispersal and the occurrence of viral co-infections, while assessing the distribution of CDV across colonies. We used metatranscriptomic sequencing to characterise the viromes of 178 live and recently deceased fur seals sampled from four large fur seal colonies (Kaik[o]ura, Dunedin, West Coast and Wairarapa). We investigated viral diversity, community composition and geographic structure using phylogenetic analyses to examine viral evolutionary relationships and CDV distribution. We identified 23 viral species, including 20 putatively novel species. Several were related to viruses previously identified in terrestrial mammals. One viral species was detected across geographically separated colonies, while several other closely related viruses were identified across colonies, with viral sharing most frequent between Kaik[o]ura and Wairarapa. Viral diversity was similar between live and recently deceased fur seals, while community composition showed geographic structuring. CDV was detected only in Kaik[o]ura, where the lineage associated with the 2024 outbreak remained in circulation. No CDV was detected in the other sampled colonies. This study reveals substantial previously undocumented viral diversity in New Zealand fur seals, improving our understanding of viral distribution and CDV circulation in marine mammal populations.

items.title: Single-cell analysis identifies concurrent type 2 and interferon programs in experimental eosinophilic esophagitis
items.blurb: Background & Aims: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, type 2 cytokine-driven allergic disease of the esophagus. How the immune and structural cell landscape of the esophagus changes between healthy and inflamed tissue requires further investigation. Methods: CD45-enriched esophageal cells from naive and oxazolone (OXA)-challenged wild-type mice were profiled by single-cell RNA sequencing. A cytokine-gated gene expression score identified type 2 program-high cells. Findings were compared with published human esophageal datasets, validated histologically, and examined in Il13ra1-/- mice. Results: A total of 62,245 esophageal cells were analyzed. ILC2s accounted for most type 2 cytokine-expressing lymphocytes in naive mice, whereas Th2 cells accounted for approximately 80% following OXA challenge. ILC2s concurrently lost Il5, Il13 and Gata3 expression while retaining Areg. Resident memory-like CD8 T cells became the largest lymphoid population. Mast cells switched from a connective tissue-type to a mucosal-type and partly cycling state, which was confirmed by increased MCPT1 cells. Esophageal eosinophils displayed a signature resembling skin eosinophils of atopic dermatitis rather than gastrointestinal eosinophils. Il13ra1-/- mice were protected from epithelial proliferation, thickening and eosinophilia. An interferon-associated program characterized lymphoid, myeloid and structural compartments, and its epithelial component was conserved in human EoE. Conclusions: Th2 cells and mucosal-type mast cells are the dominant sources of type 2 cytokines in experimental EoE. This study further identifies a conserved interferon-associated program that accompanies the type 2 response in the immune and structural compartments of the esophagus and highlights it as a candidate contributor to EoE pathology.

items.title: Prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling promotes maladaptive plasticity of direct pathway striatal projection neurons
items.blurb: As Parkinson's disease (PD) progresses and nigrostriatal dopamine (DA) neuron degeneration worsens, DA replacement therapies shift from restoring motor function to evoking dyskinesia. How disease progression mediates this transition remains poorly understood. Here, we optimized a 6-hydroxydopamine (6OHDA) model that reliably generates multiple severities of DA axon denervation within the striatum of individual mice. We identify a critical denervation threshold at which direct-pathway striatal projection neurons (dSPNs), which are key drivers of dyskinesia become pathologically hyperresponsive to DA. Using slice electrophysiology, we establish that denervation-induced increase in intrinsic excitability is insufficient to explain the aberrant response of dSPNs to DA. We further demonstrate using genetic and chemogenetic manipulations that prolonged loss of D1 receptor signaling drives the pathological transformation of dSPNs cell-autonomously, and that sustained Gs-coupled metabotropic receptor signaling in dSPNs is sufficient to both prevent and reverse it. These findings provide a mechanistic framework for understanding how PD progression renders striatal circuits vulnerable to DA-evoked motor complications and identify sustained signaling by Gs-coupled receptors as a potential avenue for preventing or reversing denervation-induced maladaptive striatal plasticity.

items.title: Preprocessing Determines Whether Fractal Biomarkers Detect Neurodegeneration: A Systematic Evaluation Across Five fMRI Pipelines
items.blurb: Fractal analysis of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) has been proposed for detecting altered neural dynamics in Alzheimers disease (AD), but the effect of preprocessing on these measurements is poorly constrained. We evaluated 229 ADNI3 participants (156 cognitively normal [CN], 60 mild cognitive impairment [MCI], and 13 AD) processed with five ENIGMA HALFpipe variants. Each scan contained 197 volumes (TR = 3.0 s) and 434 regional time series. The reported CN-AD effect varied 4.5-fold for the detrended fluctuation analysis (DFA) Hurst exponent and 13.1-fold for Sample Entropy; both measures met p < 0.05 only after aCompCor. Under aCompCor, mean H was 0.812 in CN, 0.827 in MCI, and 0.872 in AD (d = -1.40, p = 0.0003), whereas the other four DFA effects were approximately d = -0.31 to -0.40. A variance decomposition attributed 41.5% of total H variance to pipeline, 44.5% to participant, and 0.3% to diagnosis. Whole-brain analysis found higher H in AD across 16 of 18 networks, with 36 cortical regions surviving false-discovery-rate correction. Synthetic fractional Gaussian noise experiments confirmed monotonic DFA estimation at the available scan length. The small AD group makes all disease-effect estimates exploratory. These results show that preprocessing choice can determine whether fractal group differences are detectable and should therefore be treated as part of the biomarker definition.

items.title: Common organization of collective dynamics across divergent self-organized neural architectures
items.blurb: Brain organoids and other model neuronal networks build synaptic circuits through self-organization, and different protocols yield markedly different architectures, letting us test how collective dynamics depend on large-scale organization. We compared organoids of layered cortical-like structure against networks of cell-body clusters joined by axonal cables, quantifying the reproducible patterns of population activity in each. Bursts occurred in both architectures and comprised several collective patterns in each, so no single recurring template describes them. Recurrent activation sequences capture only part of this organization, sequence participation is graded, and neurons that rarely join a sequence still contribute to the shared dynamics. The patterns also pick out overlapping neuronal groups with propagation-like spatial order. Although the patterns differed between tissue models, their organization was conserved, and remained unchanged under pharmacological increases in network activity. Recurrent sequences therefore represent one manifestation of a broader collective organization that emerges across distinct self-organized neural architectures.

items.title: Body-wide microbial ecosystem reorganization across the cognitive impairment spectrum in Parkinsons disease
items.blurb: Cognitive impairment (CI) is a major determinant of disability in Parkinsons disease (PD), yet how microbial alterations across multiple body sites accompany cognitive dysfunction remains poorly understood. We characterized microbial communities from five body sites (stool, saliva, tongue, nasal cavity, and axilla) in 150 participants spanning healthy controls, PD with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI), and PD dementia (PDD), generating 616 samples for 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis v2 (MOFA2) identified a multisite microbial signature with prominent oral and gut contributions that varied across clinical groups (Factor 8; {beta} = -0.58, p < 0.0001). MintTea analysis identified stable multisite microbial assemblies associated with cognitive status, including a module distinguishing PD-MCI from PDD (in-sample AUROC = 0.810). Core microbiome analysis revealed a net reduction of 45 genus-site core memberships across four anatomical sites in cognitively impaired participants, including reduced prevalence of the butyrate-associated genus Roseburia. Multivariable models incorporating microbial signatures and demographic covariates explained an average of 35.4% of cognitive-outcome variance, with microbial features contributing an additional 8.0 percentage points beyond age, sex, and education. Procrustes analysis revealed a pronounced, non-linear pattern of weakening cross-site microbial community correspondence at the dementia stage. The Global Body-wide Organization Index remained relatively stable between HC (0.335) and PD-MCI (0.341) but declined to 0.257 in PDD, representing a 23% reduction relative to HC. Together, these findings identify disease-associated multisite microbial signatures and altered core-community composition across the PD cognitive impairment spectrum, supporting further investigation of multisite microbiome profiling for cognitive stratification.

items.title: Integrating Biometric, Metabolic, and Photochemical Traits to Identify Candidate Physiological Indicators of Salinity Tolerance and Forage Quality in Alfalfa Cultivars
items.blurb: Salinity limits alfalfa (Medicago sativa L.) productivity, yet integrative physiological markers of cultivar tolerance remain poorly defined. This study aimed to identify candidate physiological indicators of salt tolerance by integrating growth, metabolic, and time-resolved photosynthetic traits across diverse alfalfa cultivars. We exposed nine alfalfa cultivars to a 200 mM NaCl hydroponic shock and monitored their physiological responses over 14 days. We assessed shoot and root growth, leaf Na+/K+ homeostasis, carbohydrate partitioning, dynamic chlorophyll a fluorescence (ChlF), and NIRS-based forage quality. Salinity elicited cultivar-dependent responses. Tolerant cultivars maintained shoot biomass, restricted foliar Na+ accumulation, preserved leaf starch reserves, and progressively recovered Phi2 and linear electron flow (LEF) following initial declines. In contrast, less tolerant cultivars showed persistent growth inhibition, reduced leaf starch, and persistent photochemical impairment. At 7 and 14 dpt, PItotal and Fv'/Fm' correlated positively with final biomass, whereas PhiNPQ and PhiNO showed negative correlations. Notably, the association between regulated energy dissipation (PhiNPQ) and biomass retention inverted over time, shifting from an early photoprotective mechanism at 1 dpt to a sign of chronic photoinhibitory strain by 7 and 14 dpt. These responses were accompanied by cultivar-specific changes in Na+/K+; balance, soluble sugars, starch, and forage quality. Tracking time-resolved PSII photochemistry reveals that maintaining PItotal and Fv'/Fm' under saline stress offers an accurate, non-invasive proxy for evaluating cultivar resilience. Their integration into high-throughput phenotyping and breeding programs could facilitate the selection of resilient cultivars. Field validation should consider both biomass production and forage nutritional quality.

items.title: A trade-off shaping leaf mesophyll architecture emerges from a stochastic geometry model
items.blurb: Leaf mesophyll architecture has a great impact on plant functions, including photosynthesis. Yet, understanding the principles governing growth, stability, and interspecific variation of leaf mesophyll architecture remains elusive. Here, we develop a computational framework based on stochastic space tessellation to simulate two-dimensional paradermal slices of leaf spongy mesophyll across 40 vascular plant species using three data-derived parameters: leaf porosity, cell arm length, and cell arm diameter. The framework successfully reconstructs leaf slices while preserving six biological, topological, and cell-level traits, with one- to three-armed cell geometries generally outperforming circular cells. Importantly, we further develop a theoretical model based on stochastic geometry that closely agrees with the simulations and reveals that leaf porosity strongly influences cell wall construction cost, while cell-arm statistics shape this relationship. Our parsimoniously parameterized model provides a basis for optimizing leaf architecture to maximize carbon dioxide uptake while minimizing cell wall construction costs.

items.title: Feasibility of methionine oxidation quantification in proteins through Raman and FT-IR spectroscopy
items.blurb: The development of biopharmaceuticals poses unique challenges, with alterations of chemical integrity potentially impairing product efficacy and safety. Thus, oxidation-susceptibility of drug candidates is typically assessed by chromatographic methods, potentially coupled with mass spectrometry (LC-MS), which enable residue-specific oxidation monitoring but require high-resolution instrumentation, specialized expertise, and may introduce sample preparation artefacts. These constraints have raised interest in orthogonal, simple and fast methods to probe oxidation in native protein samples. Raman and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FT-IR) have shown potential for detecting methionine oxidation, the most common oxidative protein liability. The aim of this work was to transfer the known quantification potential of cuvette-based Raman spectroscopy to Raman microscopy and evaluate its suitability for high-throughput screenings. Following several technical optimizations, this work shows that the detection of oxidation by Raman microscopy could only be confirmed for molecular methionine in solution and not for proteinogenic methionine. In contrast, liquid-cell FT-IR enabled solid quantitative read-outs of methionine oxidation in proteins. Under the investigated forced degradation conditions, the method showed good agreement to orthogonal LC-MS measurements utilizing the multi-attribute method (MAM). These findings position liquid-cell FT-IR as a potential rapid, low-volume screening tool for oxidation assessments in native protein samples, particularly during early-stage biopharmaceutical development.

items.title: Proteome-scale inference of transcription factor binding motifs from predicted protein-DNA structures
items.blurb: Transcription factors (TFs) control development and cell identity by binding sequence-specific DNA motifs, yet the binding specificities of most TFs remain unknown because experimental binding assays do not scale. In zebrafish, only one-third of TFs have assigned motifs, nearly all inferred by homology from human or mouse experimental data. Here we present a proteome-scale computational screen that infers DNA-binding specificity from predicted protein-DNA structures. We use AlphaFold3 to model zebrafish TFs with candidate motif sequences derived from accessible chromatin, then use NA-MPNN to infer the DNA motifs from the most confident predictions. Across 210 TFs with experimentally characterized orthologs, predicted motifs match the known motif for 44%. Propagated through sequence clusters, these predictions form ZebraMotif, a motif database for all 2,543 zebrafish TFs. ZebraMotif covers 2.8 times as many TFs as CisBP's zebrafish collection and links accessible regulatory elements to candidate upstream regulators genome-wide. Because the approach requires only a proteome and a set of candidate motifs, it is applicable to any species lacking experimental binding data.

items.title: Haplotype reconstruction in multi-generational diploid and tetraploid populations
items.blurb: Previously, we developed a statistical framework and software (PolyOrigin1) to reconstruct parental haplotypes of each offspring in connected tetraploid F1 populations. A key application of the technology is quantitative trait loci (QTL) mapping, via regression of phenotypes on posterior probabilities of parental origins. In this work, we extend the methodology and software (PolyOrigin2) to multi-generational populations (both diploid and tetraploid), which are common in breeding programs. The extension links parental origins across generations to estimate posterior probabilities of founder origins. Compared to PolyOrigin1, the main challenge is to phase intermediate individuals that are both parents and offspring, which is overcome by the Bayesian update rule. In addition, genotypic error models are extended to account for sequencing errors such as allelic bias and overdispersion in genotyping-by-sequencing (GBS). Extensive simulations were used to compare PolyOrigin2 with previous methods and to study the effects of such variables as sequencing errors and the number of progeny per parent. We further evaluated PolyOrigin2 using three real datasets: diploid potato with 23 founders and 7 generations, tetraploid potato with 10 founders and 3 generations, and tetraploid blueberry with 10 founders and 4 generations. The results show that PolyOrigin2 is accurate for haplotype phasing and reconstruction in diploid and tetraploid pedigrees and opens new opportunities for haplotype-based QTL mapping.

items.title: Cell-type-resolved methylation analysis using bulk long-read sequencing across human tissues
items.blurb: DNA methylation shapes cellular identity and changes with aging and disease, but most human methylomes come from bulk tissue, which mixes signal across many cell types. A methylation change at the bulk tissue level can reflect a change in cellular composition or an intrinsic shift within a cell type, and the two cannot be separated from bulk data. Single-cell and sorted-cell methods resolve cell types directly, but their cost and workflow complexity pose challenges to large studies. Long-read sequencing of single DNA molecules can directly detect DNA methylation on each read. We built COMET (Cell-of-Origin from METhylation), a framework that uses cell-type-specific methylation to assign individual long reads to cell types from standard bulk long-read sequencing. COMET detects changes in cell-type composition robustly even from shallow bulk long-read data, quantifies methylation level of repetitive DNA within each cell type, and, with deeper sequencing, resolves methylation differences between health and disease in individual cell types. We applied COMET to 140 human blood samples, 104 human brain samples and 59 human colon samples. In blood, we found epigenetic aging clock is primarily driven by shifts in cell-type composition, and that APOE4 carriers have myeloid-specific methylation changes. In brain, we found sex-biased change in cell-type composition with age, resolved methylation and hydroxymethylation separately within each cell type. In colon, we found a consistent expansion of fibroblasts in tumors relative to matched normal tissue, localized methylation loss at LINE-1 in fibroblast cells, and identified tumor- and cell-type-specific hypermethylation in epithelial cells at the promoters of known colorectal cancer genes. By resolving cell-type-specific methylation directly from bulk long-read data, this approach opens broad study of cell-type epigenetics across human tissues in aging and disease.

items.title: Site-Specific and Diet-Dependent Genetic Architecture of Trabecular Bone in Male BXD Recombinant Inbred Mice
items.blurb: Vertebral fracture risk is influenced by trabecular bone (Tb) microarchitecture, a phenotype that is regulated by genetic and environmental factors. We examined the genetic architecture of Tb microarchitecture in the fifth lumbar vertebra (L5) and its modification by dietary calcium (Ca). Male mice from 51 BXD recombinant inbred lines were fed adequate (0.5%) or low (0.25%) Ca diets from 4 to 12 weeks of age. Micro-computed tomography (CT) was used to assess seven L5 Tb phenotypes, and the response to Ca restriction (RCR) was calculated for each phenotype. Quantitative trait loci (QTL) were identified by composite interval mapping and compared with previously reported femoral Tb QTL from the same mice. Genetic background significantly influenced all L5 phenotypes and their responses to Ca restriction. We identified 127 QTL distributed across 61 loci. First, very few L5 QTL overlapped those previously identified in the femur, providing strong evidence for skeletal site-specific genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture. Second, QTL detection was strongly dependent on dietary Ca, with only 4 of 33 loci identified under adequate Ca intake also detected under low Ca intake. Third, QTL controlling the RCR were largely distinct from those controlling L5 phenotypes under either dietary condition. Many loci affected multiple phenotypes, suggesting shared genetic regulation of Tb characteristics. Integration of genetic variation, expression QTL, and existing functional evidence identified plausible candidate genes at several high-priority loci. Together, these findings demonstrate that genetic regulation of Tb microarchitecture is both skeletal site-specific and diet-dependent, and that adaptation to dietary Ca restriction has a distinct genetic component.

items.title: ER-vacuole tether Mdm1 coordinates lipid homeostasis to support autophagosome formation
items.blurb: Autophagosome formation requires cells to mobilize lipids for phagophore expansion and completion while maintaining lipid homeostasis during nutrient stress. How lipid intermediates are partitioned between membrane synthesis and neutral lipid storage under these conditions remains unclear. Here, we identify ER-vacuole tether Mdm1 as a regulator of starvation-induced autophagy in budding yeast. Loss of Mdm1 reduced autophagic flux despite preserved TORC1 responses to starvation and impaired autophagosome completion, as indicated by the accumulation of perivacuolar Atg8-positive structures and reduced protease protection. Lipidomic analyses revealed decreased phosphatidylinositol (PI) in whole cells and Atg8-enriched membrane fractions, accompanied by increased diacylglycerol (DAG) and storage lipids. Derepression of phospholipid synthesis through OPI1 deletion or inhibition of triacylglycerol synthesis restored autophagic flux. Remarkably, exogenous DAG also rescued autophagy despite elevated endogenous DAG in Mdm1-deficient cells. DAG supplementation increased PI abundance and improved protease protection, linking changes in lipid metabolism to autophagosome completion. Together, these findings implicate Mdm1 in coordinating membrane phospholipid homeostasis with neutral lipid metabolism and suggest that the metabolic availability of lipid intermediates contributes to efficient autophagosome formation during starvation.

items.title: Not all plant-based diets are alike: intake of minimally processed plant foods is associated with gut microbial richness among vegetarians and vegans.
items.blurb: Plant-based diets are usually defined by what they exclude, overlooking which plant foods are eaten and how processed they are. Here we examine whether this overlooked dimension is related to the gut microbiome. In a cross-sectional study of 172 omnivorous, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and vegan adults profiled by shotgun metagenomics, vegetarians and vegans harboured fewer gut species than omnivores. Within this group, however, each standard deviation increase in minimally processed plant-food intake was associated with 27 additional species (p = 0.001), independently of fibre intake, and richness in participants with the highest intake approached that of omnivores. No such association was seen among omnivores. Higher intake was also linked to more species previously associated with favourable cardiometabolic health and to better health-related quality of life. Dietary labels alone may therefore conceal meaningful variation in the gut microbiome, and characterising how plant foods are processed may help in understanding how plant-based diets relate to health.

items.title: Depth-partitioned oxidation of atmospheric hydrogen, carbon monoxide and methane in a glacier forefield soil
items.blurb: Glacier forefields are model systems for pioneer ecosystem assembly under extreme oligotrophy. Their microbial communities carry widespread genomic potential to oxidize atmospheric trace gases, yet whether this potential is transcribed in situ, and by which lineages, remains largely untested. Here we combined depth-resolved profiling of hydrogen (H2), carbon monoxide (CO) and methane (CH4) at ten locations in the Wildstrubel glacier forefield, Swiss Alps, with mesocosm experiments, long-read metagenomics, and genome-resolved metatranscriptomics. Soils were consistent net sinks for atmospheric H2 and CH4, with fluxes ~2-fold and ~6-fold higher, respectively, in older than in younger terrain. H2 uptake was concentrated in the upper 20 cm, whereas CH4 uptake extended deeper. In the field, CO uptake was masked by apparent subsurface production, but in mesocosms lacking this source both CO and H2 were drawn below atmospheric concentrations. Although 57% of metagenome-assembled genomes encoded trace-gas oxidation enzymes, topsoil transcription was dominated by Group 1h [NiFe]-hydrogenases from a few Actinomycetota populations, in which the CO dehydrogenase coxL was transcribed 20- to 35-fold less. The second most transcribed marker was smoX, most closely related to C2-C6 alkane monooxygenases, suggesting the use of short-chain alkanes of possible subsurface origin. Mobile genetic elements were widely transcribed, matching host transcription, but a 104-kb plasmid-borne coxMSL operon was largely silent. Acetylene perturbation induced no detectable switching between trace-gas pathways. Together, these data suggest that trace-gas metabolism is partitioned across soil depth: atmospheric H2 scavenging dominates topsoil transcription, whereas methanotrophy and CO production occur deeper. Net surface fluxes, particularly for CO, therefore, underestimate gross trace-gas turnover.

items.title: Flow Virometry-Based Profiling of Viral Population Diversity
items.blurb: Viruses exhibit great phenotypic heterogeneity. Flow virometry enables high-throughput analysis of phenotypic diversity in viral populations, while flow-based sorting allows subpopulations to be isolated for separate characterization. Despite their advantages, flow virometry and sorting have not yet been widely adopted in virology partly because of limited protocols and underexplored applications. Here, we provide a practical guide for analyzing and quantifying virus particles from diverse families using flow virometry enhanced by fluorescence labeling. We further explore applications beyond basic and static characterization of virus populations. We demonstrate that flow virometry can report on interactions between virions and binding partners, as well as between virions. It provides a particle denominator that, combined with genome copy measurements, enables estimation of viral population ploidy. We also show how dynamic processes, such as viral membrane fusion, can be measured in real time. Finally, we demonstrate the feasibility of sorting virions based on their intrinsic properties, such as morphology, for downstream study. This practical guide provides a roadmap for wider implementation of flow virometry in virology, while the applications illustrated here demonstrate potential to address a variety of questions about virion properties, interactions, and dynamics at the single-particle level.

items.title: Expanded representation and function of PDF neurons in the mosquito circadian network
items.blurb: Female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes can transmit pathogens when they bite humans, their preferred hosts, and this host-seeking drive is tightly gated by time of day. Daily rhythms depend on the molecular clock and communication among clock neurons, yet mosquito circadian network organization remains poorly understood. Using a mosquito-specific PERIOD antibody, we mapped the putative clock network of Aedes aegypti and found that neurons expressing the neuropeptide Pigment-Dispersing Factor (PDF) make up a much larger proportion of clock neurons compared to other insects, indicating a divergent network organization. PDF neurons are required for normal rhythms across insects, but whether their importance scales with their abundance in the network is unknown. We therefore tested the functional role of this expanded PDF neuron population in mosquitoes: we show that electrically silencing Aedes aegypti PDF neurons abolished the separation of daily activity into morning and evening peaks and led to misaligned clock protein rhythms across circadian neurons, even under entraining light-dark cycles. Thus, in a network built around an unusually large PDF population, PDF neuron activity plays an outsized role in behavioral timing and network synchrony.

items.title: Rage bait: a neurofunctional signature of moral outrage elicited by social media
items.blurb: Moral outrage is ubiquitous online, with powerful emotional and motivational consequences for social life. Combining naturalistic fMRI during exposure to short-form social-media videos depicting moral violations with predictive modeling, we developed a neurofunctional signature of subjective moral outrage (MONS) in discovery/validation (n=80/30) cohorts. MONS predicted experienced outrage and punishment tendencies across cohorts. Positive predictive weights encompassed regions implicated in mentalizing, threat detection and action initiation (precuneus, posterior cingulate, periaqueductal gray, hypothalamus, cerebellum), whereas negative weights involved valuation and behavioral flexibility systems (amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex).
