items.title: DR Congo: The Bundibugyo Ebola Outbreak in Africa: Six-Month Situation and Response Report
items.blurb:
Countries: Democratic Republic of the Congo, Kenya, Nigeria, Uganda
Source: Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention

Executive summary

This report examines the Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak and the continental response from the declaration on 15 May 2026 to the evidence available for preparation of the six-month milestone on 15 November. It integrates pathogen and transmission knowledge, zoonotic origin and One Health, epidemiology, clinical care, operational performance, country experiences, research, financing, logistics, essential health services, social consequences and preparedness.

The principal finding is that substantial response capacity was mobilized, but persistent transmission and mortality indicate that this capacity did not consistently translate into sufficiently early detection, timely access to care, complete identification of transmission networks and reliable local service delivery in DRC. The introduction that began the outbreak also remains unexplained, so the risk of further spillover in the affected landscape persists independently of progress against human-to-human transmission.

Key findings that should guide the next phase

1. The burden remains overwhelmingly concentrated in the DRC. Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria provide distinct experiences of managing cross-border or travel-associated infection. Their outcomes should be assessed against their own case histories and observation periods. France’s imported case and medical evacuations to other countries belong in a separate international account so that the same patient is not counted twice.

2. Early growth was exceptional, but historical comparison requires matched definitions. The early reported burden substantially exceeded burden observed during the comparable early periods of major 2014 and 2018 Ebola epidemics, although direct quantitative comparison is constrained by differences in case categories included, uncertainties in disease onset and official detection and declaration, ascertainment and observation intervals. Historical comparisons should therefore preserve the original case classifications and reporting periods.

3. Contact tracing misses most new cases: Only 11% of confirmed cases (1,146 of 10,659 with onset from week 19 to week 45) came from the contact lists, against a target of 95%. The response found the other 89% outside those lists, which means many transmission links were identified too late to list and monitor the contacts. The daily contact follow-up [text continues beyond the visible page].

Five headline numbers in the analytical snapshot

By 8 November 2026, five countries had reported 11,021 confirmed cases and 5,358 deaths, a crude case-fatality ratio (CFR) of 48.6%.

The DRC carries almost all of this burden, with 10,990 cases and 5,354 deaths (CFR 48.7%). Uganda reported 20 cases and 2 deaths, Kenya 9 and 2, Nigeria 1 imported case and no deaths, and France 1 imported case and no deaths.

In the DRC, 67 health zones in eight provinces have reported at least one confirmed case, and 51 of 67 health zones reported a case in the last 21 days.

National notifications have held at about 460 to 480 confirmed cases a week since late September; the epidemic is a sustained plateau and not yet declining.

items.title: Lebanon: Gender-Based Violence Information Management System (GBVIMS) - Midyear Report 2026
items.blurb:
Country: Lebanon
Sources: UN High Commissioner for Refugees, United Nations Population Fund

Please refer to the attached file.

The Gender-Based Violence Information Management System (GBVIMS) Midyear Report 2026 presents an analysis of GBV incidents reported to 18 participating service providers across Lebanon between January and June 2026, comparing findings with the same period in 2025. The report examines trends in reported incidents, survivor profiles, displacement-related risks, access to services, and referral gaps against the backdrop of renewed hostilities, widespread displacement, and increasing humanitarian needs.

The report identifies a 32% decrease in reported GBV incidents compared with the first half of 2025. However, this decline should not be interpreted as a reduction in GBV prevalence. Conflict-related disruptions, reduced availability of services, funding constraints, displacement, and barriers to safe disclosure have affected survivors' ability to access assistance and report incidents.

Key findings include:

  • Women and girls accounted for 99% of reported survivors, while adults represented 92% of survivors.
  • Intimate partner violence (IPV) remained the predominant case context, accounting for 90% of reported incidents, with a 9% increase in reported IPV cases compared with midyear 2025.
  • Psychological/emotional abuse (39%) and physical assault (38%) were the most frequently reported forms of GBV.
  • Internally displaced persons accounted for 20% of reported survivors, highlighting the impact of renewed hostilities and displacement on protection risks and access to services.
  • Nearly one-third of survivors (29%) sought assistance more than one month after the incident, reflecting persistent barriers to timely reporting and support.
  • Significant service gaps remain, including limited access to specialized mental health services, with 52% of mental health referrals reported as unavailable, alongside gaps in livelihoods and recovery support.

The findings highlight how conflict, displacement, economic hardship, and reductions in humanitarian funding continue to affect GBV risks and survivors' access to essential services. The report calls for strengthened GBV risk mitigation in displacement settings, sustained survivor-centred case management and referral services, improved access to specialized mental health and economic recovery support, and greater investment in preventing and responding to intimate partner violence.

The report aims to inform evidence-based humanitarian programming, coordination, advocacy, and resource allocation to ensure continued access to safe, confidential, and quality GBV services across Lebanon.

Data limitation: GBVIMS findings reflect incidents reported by survivors who accessed participating service providers and consented to the anonymized use of their information. They do not represent the total number of GBV incidents or measure GBV prevalence in Lebanon.

items.title: World: ICRC: Explosive remnants of war continue to kill and maim civilians long after the fighting ends
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

Statement on the occasion of 20th Annual Conference of the High-Contracting Parties to Protocol V of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, 12 November 202

In many parts of the world, explosive remnants of war litter cities, agricultural fields and countrysides that are no longer battlefields. They continue to kill and maim thousands of civilians every year despite active hostilities having ended long ago. According to the Landmine and Cluster Munitions Monitor, in 2025, a large proportion of victims of mines, cluster munitions and explosive remnants of war were children.

In our work in armed conflicts around the world, we witness every day how explosive remnants of war impede access to health-care facilities and other essential services. They block transport and escape routes, hinder the delivery of life-saving humanitarian assistance and hamper agriculture and trade. In post-conflict settings, explosive remnants of war delay reconstruction efforts and prevent the return of displaced people to their home areas. In 2024, according to the Landmine Monitor, 52 states and territories remained affected by anti-personnel mines and other explosive remnants of war. This indicates the magnitude of the issue.

Mr. President,

The use of heavy explosive weapons in populated areas multiplies the human cost of conflict, including by leaving behind explosive remnants of war that continue to endanger civilians long after the fighting has ended. Historic and recent conflicts are clear examples.

The ICRC and the wider International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement call on all states and parties to armed conflict to avoid the use of explosive weapons with a wide impact area in populated areas. This means that these weapons should not be used in populated areas unless sufficient mitigation measures can be taken to reduce the weapons’ wide-area effects and the consequent risk of civilian harm. The landmark Political Declaration on Strengthening the Protection of Civilians from the Humanitarian Consequences Arising from the Use of Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas, which, to date, has been endorsed by 91 states, marks significant progress in this respect. We encourage all states to endorse the Declaration and to implement it effectively. Furthermore, and given the significant presence of civilians in urban areas, we urge states to make particular efforts to ensure full compliance with their obligations under Protocol V when using explosive weapons in cities or other populated areas.

Mr. President,

Approximately half the world's states are party to Protocol V. The rate of its universalization has slowed down but not stalled completely. We would like to congratulate Serbia, which has consented to be bound by Protocol V and look forward to their becoming the 100th state party to the Protocol in March 2027. We urge all states that are not yet party to Protocol V to adhere to it and we remind all States Parties to remain steadfast in implementing their obligations under it.

In the past year, the ICRC has promoted Protocol V to states bilaterally and at regional forums in South Asia, South-East Asia and the Caribbean.

Mr. President,

Today, the ICRC partners with 20 National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, with more than 2,100 staff and volunteers, working alongside communities to help reduce their exposure to the risks posed by mines, cluster munitions and other explosive remnants of war. This work includes technical support in clearance operations, raising awareness of and promoting safe behaviour, physical rehabilitation services, and support for the social and economic inclusion of survivors.

Our Advisory Service on IHL and colleagues in New York, Geneva and in ICRC delegations in capital cities around the world stand ready to continue assisting states in joining and implementing the Protocol.

items.title: Pakistan: Inter-Agency Winterization Strategy 2026 - 2027
items.blurb:
Country: Pakistan
Sources: International Organization for Migration, UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

1. General

Pakistan experiences winter conditions primarily from November to February, with severe cold and snowfall concentrated in northern and high-altitude regions. Winter-related hazards include cold waves, heavy snowfall, avalanches, landslides, blizzards and fog, with varying impacts across the country. Mountainous areas face extreme temperatures and seasonal isolation, while communities in the plains may experience cold nights and damp conditions.

While Pakistan did not experience a major nationwide climate-related disaster in 2026 comparable to the previous year's floods, localized flooding affected parts of Gilgit-Baltistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab and Balochistan, resulting in localized damage to housing, infrastructure and livelihoods. An earthquake in the Upper Hunza area near the Wakhan Corridor further heightened concerns for affected mountain communities, where prolonged winters, sub-zero temperatures and seasonal access restrictions can significantly increase exposure risks. Households with damaged or inadequate shelters, particularly those in remote high-altitude settlements, may face heightened vulnerabilities during winter 2026–27. These localized impacts, together with residual vulnerabilities from previous disasters, reinforce the need for geographically targeted gender and age-responsive winterization assistance based on verified household needs and current shelter conditions.

According to NDMA's Disaster Early Warning–4 (DEW-4), October–December 2026, seasonal snow cover is projected to expand progressively across the Hindu Kush, Karakoram and western Himalayan ranges, beginning in October and becoming more extensive and persistent during November and December. The principal areas of concern include Gilgit-Baltistan, Upper Chitral, high-altitude districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and mountainous areas of Azad Jammu and Kashmir. Western Disturbances are expected to remain the primary drivers of significant snowfall episodes, while broader climate variability, including the El Niño– Southern Oscillation (ENSO), may influence seasonal weather patterns. Successive snowfall events, persistent freezing conditions and localized avalanche risks could disrupt road connectivity, restrict humanitarian access and isolate remote communities, particularly along high-altitude transport corridors.

These projections, together with seasonal advisories from PMD and consultations with PDMAs, GBDMA and SDMA, provide the basis for geographically differentiated winter-risk assessments and prioritization for 2026– 27.

Purpose of the Collective AAP Platform

The South Sudan Collective AAP Platform will strengthen how AAP data (what communities are telling us and asking us to act on) is systematically brought into strategic and operational decisionmaking.

The Platform will consolidate existing de-identified AAP data from a range of sources into a format that allows us to identify trends, identify emerging issues, and inform programmatic adjustments at the inter-agency level, and ensure that decisions from leadership are influenced by community data. The responsibility for addressing individual complaints remains with individual organisations. The Platform should not duplicate efforts or be a parallel system to existing practices.

The intention is for the Platform to be a simple tool that is not an onerous additional stream of reporting for contributing organisations. It seeks to complement existing systems, enabling the trends in what communities are telling us to have a wider and more influential reach.

It provides aggregate information on trends, and is not designed, or intended, to single out individual organisations.

  • Según cifras oficiales, desde el 29 de agosto de 2026, las lluvias asociadas al fenómeno de El Niño han dejado más de 80.000 personas impactadas y afectaciones a 166 cantones y 508 parroquias, con predominio de inundaciones (57%) y deslizamientos (17%).
  • Los pronósticos del Comité Nacional para el Estudio Regional del Fenómeno El Niño (CN-ERFEN) y del Centro Internacional para la Investigación del Fenómeno de El Niño (CIIFEN) indican que El Niño continúa fortaleciéndose y podría alcanzar una intensidad fuerte a muy fuerte entre finales de 2026 e inicios de 2027, aumentando el riesgo de lluvias intensas, inundaciones y crecidas de ríos, particularmente en la región Costa.
  • Las evaluaciones preliminares realizadas en territorios afectados identifican necesidades prioritarias en alojamiento, agua, saneamiento e higiene, salud, seguridad alimentaria, protección y recuperación temprana, especialmente entre hogares que han sufrido daños en sus viviendas y pérdida de bienes esenciales.
  • El Gobierno mantiene la Alerta Roja nacional por el fenómeno de El Niño y coordina la respuesta a través de 215 Comités de Operaciones de Emergencias (en adelante COE) activos, mientras que la asistencia humanitaria entregada supera los 60.000 bienes de ayuda distribuidos por la SNGR y las instituciones del Sistema Nacional Descentralizado de Gestión Integral de Riesgos y Desastres (en adelante SNDGIRD).(34.130 por La Secretaría Nacional de Gestión de Riesgos- SNGR y 26.794 por el SNDGIRD).

RESUMEN DE LA SITUACIÓN

Las lluvias asociadas al fortalecimiento del fenómeno de El Niño continúan generando afectaciones en Ecuador. Desde el 29 de agosto hasta el 17 de noviembre de 2026, según cifras oficiales, se han registrado al menos 83.975 personas impactadas (51.095 afectadas y 32.880 damnificadas), además, se reportan 1.500 eventos adversos relacionados con precipitaciones en las 24 provincias, afectando a 166 cantones y 508 parroquias. Las inundaciones representan el 57% de los eventos reportados, seguidas por deslizamientos (17%), lluvias intensas (7%) y vendavales (6%). Las provincias con mayor impacto en la población son Esmeraldas, Guayas, El Oro, Los Ríos, Santa Elena, Manabí, Galápagos y Bolívar.

De acuerdo con el Comité Nacional para el Estudio Regional del Fenómeno El Niño (CN-ERFEN), las condiciones oceánicas y atmosféricas continúan mostrando el fortalecimiento del evento, con una probabilidad superior al 83% de que alcance una intensidad fuerte a muy fuerte durante los próximos meses. Este escenario coincide con los análisis del Centro Internacional para la Investigación del Fenómeno de El Niño (CIIFEN), que identifica el periodo entre octubre y diciembre de 2026 como la fase de mayor intensidad del fenómeno, aumentando el riesgo de lluvias por encima de lo normal, inundaciones y crecidas de ríos en la región Costa.

En respuesta al incremento de las afectaciones, las autoridades nacionales y locales han fortalecido las acciones de preparación y respuesta, incluyendo la activación de mecanismos de coordinación de emergencia, la emisión de alertas y declaratorias correspondientes, así como la movilización de asistencia humanitaria para las poblaciones afectadas. De manera paralela, las instituciones del sistema nacional de gestión de riesgos mantienen el monitoreo de las condiciones hidrometeorológicas y de la evolución del fenómeno de El Niño, con el fin de anticipar impactos y ampliar las capacidades de respuesta en los territorios de mayor exposición.

During October, Mali continued to face persistent instability and complex protection challenges, including the forced recruitment of young people, widespread displacement of communities, and gender-based violence.

While the reopening of transit routes into Léré marked a significant improvement in humanitarian access for relief operations, comprehensive rapid assessments revealed critical gaps in front-line health facilities. These included severe shortages of basic pharmaceutical supplies, prohibitive out-of-pocket medical expenses, and an acute deficit of trained healthcare workers.

In response to the escalating hostilities and growing humanitarian needs, UNFPA rapidly scaled up its emergency response, expanding access to life-saving assistance across key locations through fixed and mobile service delivery points. Supported by 37 deployed community midwives, integrated mobile teams conducted extensive outreach to displacement sites and facilitated referrals to health facilities across Léré, Niafunké, Tonka, Macina, San, and Gao. Through these coordinated efforts, UNFPA provided essential sexual and reproductive health services to 16,024 people and reached more than 11,290 people with gender-based violence risk mitigation, comprehensive care, and protection services during the month.

items.title: Myanmar: UN Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Sexual Violence in Conflict, Pramila Patten, welcomes landmark judgment of the International Court of Justice on genocide against the Rohingya
items.blurb:
Countries: Myanmar, Bangladesh
Source: UN Office of the SRSG on Sexual Violence in Conflict

Press Release: For Immediate Release

New York, 19 November 2026: The Special Representative of the Secretary-General on Sexual Violence in Conflict welcomes the historic judgment of the International Court of Justice in The Gambia v. Myanmar, finding that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. The Court’s recognition of the extensive acts of rape and other forms of sexual violence during so-called clearance operations by Myanmar’s armed forces often accompanied by extreme physical brutality resulted in lasting physical harm to reproductive functioning and psychological trauma, as well as social ostracism. This judgment stands as a testament to the courage and perseverance of survivors who, despite trauma, stigma and personal risk, came forward to testify and engage with accountability mechanisms.

“When I first met with Rohingya survivors of sexual violence in Cox’s Bazaar in 2017, their testimonies of rape and gang rape while tied to rocks and trees, which forced entire communities to flee their homes and homelands shook me to my core. Today’s recognition by the world’s highest court of the extensive sexual violence committed against them is a vital acknowledgement of the crimes they endured and underscores that sexual violence must not be overlooked or treated as incidental to mass atrocities that can constitute genocide.”

Special Representative Patten calls on Myanmar to swiftly and fully comply with the Court’s judgment, and on the international community to support its implementation, while drawing particular attention to the Court’s order for rehabilitative measures and the significance of these orders for survivors of sexual violence who deserve recognition, redress and a future free from violence and fear.

The Myanmar armed forces, including the integrated border guard, remain listed by the Secretary-General in the annex to his annual report to the United Nations Security Council on conflict-related sexual violence for committing or being responsible for patterns of rape or other forms of sexual violence in armed conflict.

Special Representative Patten stated: “Today’s judgment must mark not only a turning point in the pursuit of justice for past crimes, but also a catalyst of the prevention of future atrocities. The true measure of this historic judgment will be the extent to which it transforms the lives of survivors and future generations. Justice must not only be pronounced in The Hague; it must be felt in the lives of the Rohingya people.”

For media inquiries, please contact:

Ms. Géraldine Boezio, Office of the Special Representative on Sexual Violence in Conflict

Email: geraldine.boezio@un.org

items.title: Update 376 – IAEA Director General Statement on Situation in Ukraine
items.blurb:
Country: Ukraine
Source: International Atomic Energy Agency

As Ukraine enters the winter period, the challenges facing Ukraine’s power system are becoming even more acute, with the electrical grid in its worst condition since the start of the conflict, IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi informed the IAEA Board of Governors this week.

Fluctuations in the power output of operating units at Ukraine’s nuclear power plants (NPPs) continued this week due to the grid instability resulting from reported military activity. Furthermore, one NPP site reported the loss of one off-site power line multiple times, while another site also reported the loss of one of their off-site power lines.

Military activity continued to be reported at the Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) and around Ukraine’s other nuclear sites this week, with IAEA teams reporting repeated air raid alarms. IAEA teams at the Khmelnytskyy, Rivne and South Ukraine NPPs had to shelter. In total, 153 air raid alarms were reported, while numerous drones were detected in the vicinity of NPPs, including 86 near the Chornobyl site, and drones were also detected near to the Centralised Spent Fuel Storage Facility located in the Chornobyl Exclusion Zone. At the South Ukraine site, 23 drones were detected, while ten were detected at the Khmelnytskyy NPP and one at the Rivne NPP.

“Daily air raid alarms, at times causing the IAEA on-site teams to shelter, increasing reports of drones nearby, and continuing damage to the electrical grid all place additional pressure on plant operations,” Director General Grossi said. “I once again call for the end of military activity near all nuclear facilities. As I have said before: no one benefits from a nuclear disaster.”

“While these events did not result in a reactor trip or some other nuclear safety event, they continue to place further burden on plant staff and equipment in an already challenging situation,” Director General Grossi added.

At the ZNPP over this past weekend, a brief fault on the Ferosplavna-1 330 kilovolt (kV) power line resulted in the tripping of one of the power lines connecting the ZNPP to the electrical switchyard, which receives power from this off-site line. While the back-up line functioned as expected and emergency diesel generators were not activated, diesel fuel levels remain a significant concern should another extended loss of off-site power occur.

The IAEA staff at the ZNPP completed their most comprehensive review of available diesel fuel to date, reporting on emergency diesel generators, mobile diesel boilers used for heating and diesel steam generators used for wastewater treatment.

“We were fortunate that this past weekend’s near miss did not result in a loss of off-site power at the ZNPP, which would have put further stress on the site’s already limited diesel supplies,” the Director General said. “A new ceasefire, the ninth, is being discussed for the repair of the Dniprovska substation and the 750 kV power line. Air strikes have thwarted the efforts made over the past several months to secure the second off-site power line before winter.”

IAEA assistance to Ukraine

The IAEA continues to provide large-scale technical assistance to support nuclear safety and security in Ukraine. This week, three buses were delivered to the Chornobyl NPP to support the safe and reliable transport of staff amidst the ongoing conflict. The delivery was made possible with funds from Japan, Norway and the United Kingdom. Since the start of the conflict, emergency equipment valued at more than €28 million has been delivered to nearly 50 beneficiaries across Ukraine.

items.title: World: Oxfam reaction to the ongoing deadlock at the COP31 negotiations
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Oxfam

Reacting to ongoing deadlock at the COP31 negotiations, Nafkote Dabi, Climate Policy Lead at Oxfam International said: “With just hours left of COP31, talks are being held to ransom by rich polluting countries, including EU countries. Every hour that deliberations stall is another hour that droughts rage, floods devastate, and people cannot access resources to recover from disasters. These talks are meant to protect communities bearing the brunt of the climate crisis. They cannot afford this COP to fail.

“There is still time for real progress, and we have the solutions. At a minimum, rich countries must agree on a plan to deliver $300 billion in climate finance, including tripling adaptation funding to $120 billion, which they already agreed to do in previous COPs. Communities need this right now, not when the EU and other rich countries decide the time is right. El Niño is already intensifying – potentially into one of the strongest ever – and we’re expecting a warming overshoot of 1.7 degrees next year. This will bring devastating impacts for communities already paying for a crisis they did little to create. The countries most responsible for the climate crisis owe a climate debt, and it’s time to pay up.”

Download Oxfam’s report “Disaster Divide.”

items.title: Sudan - Concept of Operations, October 2026
items.blurb:
Country: Sudan
Sources: Logistics Cluster, World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

Content

Background

Since the outbreak of conflict between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in April 2023, Sudan has faced one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises. Nearly 8.9 million people are internally displaced – including more than 6.6 million displaced since the conflict began. This represents a 23 percent decrease from the peak of almost 11.6 million recorded in January 2025, reflecting increased returns, particularly to Khartoum and Al Jazirah. Nearly 4.6 million people have fled to neighbouring countries. The crisis has also exacerbated the humanitarian situation in Chad and South Sudan, both of which were already dealing with protracted emergencies.

In 2026, 33.7 million people in Sudan require humanitarian assistance – an increase of 3.3 million from 2025. Despite these overwhelming needs, access constraints, bureaucratic and administrative impediments, an overstretched logistics market, storage constraints, and rising costs for logistics services continue to hinder the delivery of humanitarian assistance to affected populations. Crossline and cross-border movement of humanitarian personnel and supplies continue to face significant obstacles.

To address these logistical challenges and mitigate disruptions to the humanitarian supply chain, the Logistics Cluster has been scaling up its operations since 2023 (following its initial activation in 2020). With the main operational cell based in Port Sudan, the Logistics Cluster leads coordination, advocates for the uninterrupted flow of assistance, and supports humanitarian partners operating across the country.

Operational Constraints

Humanitarian organizations are facing significant operational challenges due to factors including movement restrictions, airspace closures, limited safe access to conflict-affected areas, complex deconfliction processes, bureaucratic impediments, and telecommunications constraints, among others. These issues are significantly hindering the delivery of assistance to affected populations.

Partners have reported the following logistics gaps and bottlenecks impacting their operations, including through the Gaps and Needs Analysis (GNA) published in August 2025:

  • Limited humanitarian access to hard-to-reach areas, particularly in Darfur and Kordofan regions.
  • Limited operational points of entry into Sudan and restrictions on crossline movements due to ongoing conflict and insecurity.
  • Limited ability to contract reliable transportation and storage services due to security constraints, an overstretched market, rising costs, and service disruptions.
  • Insufficient temperature-controlled storage and transport capacity, particularly for cross-border corridors.
  • Limited information on logistics service providers’ availability and capacity, market conditions, and road network and infrastructure status, particularly during the rainy season.
  • Bureaucratic and administrative impediments, including lengthy and frequently changing customs and importation procedures and travel permit approval delays.
  • Airspace closure except for limited air access in Port Sudan, Khartoum, Kassala, and Dongola.
  • Limited fuel availability and rising costs in certain areas.

For detailed and up-to-date information on ports, airports, border crossings, and other logistics infrastructure, partners are encouraged to consult the Sudan Logistics Capacity Assessment (LCA).

items.title: Myanmar: ICJ judgment marks historic step towards justice for the Rohingya [EN/MY]
items.blurb:
Country: Myanmar
Source: UN Human Rights Council

Please refer to the attached file.

Statement by Nicholas Koumjian, Head of the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar

Geneva, 19 November 2026 – The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has today found that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, and it has been ordered to make reparations. This judgment by the world's highest court acknowledges the immense suffering endured by the Rohingya and represents a landmark step towards accountability and redress for one of the gravest crimes under international law.

The Court also found that Myanmar failed to prevent and punish genocide in breach of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. This was based on convincing evidence of brutal violence against the Rohingya in Northern Rakhine State during the 2017 clearance operations. This included large-scale killings and sexual violence, and the systematic destruction of Rohingya villages. The Court noted that, in its deliberations, the judges gave considerable evidentiary weight to the witness statements collected by the Mechanism and the six analytical reports it produced due to the demanding methodology it applied.

The Court has ordered Myanmar to investigate and prosecute those responsible, facilitate the safe and voluntary return of the Rohingya to their place of origin, return all property and provide adequate compensation for the damage caused. Within two years, Myanmar must submit a report to the Court on the measure of restitution it has adopted and the amounts and modalities of compensation.

The Mechanism recognizes both the courage of the survivors who shared their experiences and the careful deliberation reflected in the Court's decision. The proceedings involved years of legal argument and factual analysis, thousands of pages of submissions and evidence, three weeks of hearings, the oral testimony of four witnesses, and interventions by 11 States on the interpretation of the Genocide Convention.

While the Mechanism will need time to examine the judgment and its implications closely, its significance for the Rohingya is already clear. The judgment recognizes the discrimination, persecution and crimes they have suffered over many years. It also brings renewed hope that their plight has not been forgotten and high expectations that Myanmar will implement the judgment.

These proceedings concerned crimes committed against the Rohingya, yet the significance of the judgment extends beyond a single community. Many of the actors and State institutions examined by the Court are also relevant to other serious international crimes that are being committed across Myanmar.

The judgment is a major milestone, but it is not the end of the accountability process. The Court has addressed Myanmar's responsibility as a State under international law in relation to allegations of genocide. Establishing the criminal responsibility of individual perpetrators requires separate criminal investigations and judicial proceedings. The pursuit of accountability must also extend to crimes against humanity and war crimes. The Mechanism will continue to impartially investigate serious international crimes committed across Myanmar, against victims from all communities and by perpetrators of any affiliation, and support efforts to bring the individuals most responsible to justice.

The Court has now delivered its judgment. What matters next is action. Although this judgment addresses crimes committed in the past, its relevance is not confined to history. Many Rohingya continue to face the consequences of those crimes today. Myanmar must fulfil its obligations as ordered by the Court. The international community, especially States, must build on the Court's findings, demand compliance with the orders and continue to support efforts to achieve accountability and justice.

The Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM or Mechanism) was created by the United Nations Human Rights Council in 2018 to collect and analyse evidence of the most serious international crimes and other violations of international law committed in Myanmar since 2011. It aims to facilitate justice and accountability by preserving and organizing this evidence and preparing analysis that can be used by authorities to prosecute individuals in national, regional and international courts.

For more information, visit iimm.un.org or contact iimm@un.org.

items.title: How a 7-Member Team Won $15,000 for Its Work to Protect Tamil Nadu’s Tamiraparani
items.blurb: An old man in Tirunelveli remembers a time when he could bend down, collect water in his hands and drink directly from the Tamiraparani. The water, he recalls, tasted sweeter then. Today, he wouldn't do that. For Sneha Shahi, a researcher who has spent nearly five years studying the river, this recollection was more than an evocative memory. It echoed what scientific readings were beginning to reveal about the changing river. "When I really thought about it, our scientific readings of dissolved oxygen and TDS were also indicating that there's more pollution in the water now as compared to the past. We were able to link those two things together," she tells The Better India . It raised a question that would eventually shape the RE-Verse Initiative: before attempting to restore a river, do we really know what we are restoring, what has changed, and what the river needs? Today, Sneha, 29, and her younger collaborator, Vidhya Vigashini, 24, are attempting to answer that question along a 30-km stretch of the Tamiraparani in Tamil Nadu. Sneha leads research design, scientific assessments and workshops. Vidhya handles community engagement and translations, helping bridge the gap between researchers and Tamil-speaking residents. In July 2026, the Tamiraparani received legal personhood, making it the third river in India to receive such recognition. The development gives the river a distinct legal identity and brings its rights into discussions about conservation and governance. What if a river had rights of its own? Imagine someone throwing sewage into your home, cutting through your property or fundamentally changing the place where you live. These would be violations of your rights. Now imagine applying the same principle to a river. Sneha explains river personhood through precisely this comparison. "If you throw ink at a human being, that's a violation. The same goes for throwing sewage into a river. That's a violation of its right to live. If you cut a person's finger, that's a violation of human rights. In the same way, if you cut the river and re-channel it, reshape it completely, that's a violation of the natural entity." The idea is to recognise a river as an entity with rights of its own, rather than merely a resource that can be extracted, redirected or polluted. The philosophy also has parallels with the beliefs of several Indigenous communities , which have traditionally regarded rivers, hills and other natural systems as living entities with spiritual significance. The idea behind river personhood is to recognise a river as an entity with rights of its own, rather than merely a resource that can be extracted, redirected or polluted. Legal personhood, however, takes this recognition into the realm of governance. "A lot of tribes in the world also believe that natural systems like rivers and hills have a soul residing within them. But providing personhood is a more legal document, where the government is saying that the river has its rights," Sneha explains. Sneha points to the continuing pollution of the Ganga and Yamuna despite their earlier personhood-related legal recognition as a reminder of the gap between declaring rights and enforcing them. "The effects of it have yet to roll into on-ground implementation," she says of the Tamiraparani's recent recognition. For the RE-Verse team, the challenge is to ensure that the idea of river rights translates into sustained action on the ground. Before restoring a river, first understand it The RE-Verse Initiative began taking shape around three years ago. Sneha, who was pursuing her PhD on the Tamiraparani at the Ashoka Trust for Research in Ecology and the Environment (ATREE) , had put out a call for interns during her fieldwork. Vidhya, who belongs to the landscape, responded. After working together for a few months, the two realised that their skills complemented each other. Along with four other young team members, they formalised their work into a seven-member team. Sneha leads research design, scientific assessments and workshops. Vidhya handles community engagement and translations, helping bridge the gap between researchers and Tamil-speaking residents. Their work spans three locations: Aladiyur, Cheranmahadevi and Gopalasamudram. Rather than beginning with a predetermined restoration plan, the team developed a riverbank assessment sheet to document the condition of different sections. They look at the physical characteristics of the river, including its width, movement and floodplain. They also document the vegetation along its banks, identifying native plants as well as invasive species. Water hyacinth, for instance, accumulates wherever the flowing river becomes shallow or water pools. "Once invasive vegetation grows — a plant that was not supposed to be there from the beginning — it changes the actual food web and the structure of that place. Animals and insects that didn't rely on it before now become reliant on it. Slowly, everything in the structure starts to change," Sneha says. Another invasive plant they have documented is Prosopis juliflora , commonly known as mesquite. The team also studies the river's fish populations. Among the species of interest is Dawkinsia tambraparniei , a small endemic barb found in the Tamiraparani. Although small, these fish form part of a larger food web, supporting bigger fish and, indirectly, predators such as otters. The increasing presence of invasive African catfish is another concern. Rather than beginning with a predetermined restoration plan, the team developed a riverbank assessment sheet to document the condition of different sections. Sneha says recreational fishers have also expressed concern about the species. Some kill the catfish they catch because they fear its growing numbers could affect populations of edible fish. And then there are the otters. Locally known as Neer Nai, literally translating to water dog, otters were historically found along the Tamiraparani. Sneha says older researchers at ATREE had documented their presence in the landscape, but sightings have now become rare. The assessment also documents human activity: sand mining, bathing, washing, temples, sewage treatment infrastructure and the ways in which villages access river water. The objective is to understand the river as an interconnected ecosystem. The river's memory is written into its banks One of the more unusual aspects of the RE-Verse Initiative is its decision to use these traditional stone structures as potential community monitoring points. Locally, residents have told the researchers that some mandapams date back to the Chola dynasty, although the team is still investigating their precise history. A mandapam is a traditional stone pavilion found along the riverfront. Some of these structures have stood beside the Tamiraparani for generations. Sneha noticed during fieldwork that people often recognised these structures more readily than they recognised individual stretches of the river. The mandapams, therefore, offered familiar landmarks around which communities could organise their relationship with the river. The team is mapping how many structures still stand, which have fallen into disuse and which have become part of the debris along the riverbank. Where a structure remains usable without significant restoration, the researchers hope to propose it as a monitoring point. A mandapam is a traditional stone pavilion found along the riverfront. Some of these structures have stood beside the Tamiraparani for generations. The idea is that residents could visit the same mandapam every fortnight or once a month and photograph the river from the same position. Over time, these photographs could reveal changes in water levels, vegetation, erosion, waste accumulation and the riverbank itself. "You can go to this particular spot every two weeks or every month, and you can take a picture from the same place. You can then yourself see how the river changes over time," Sneha explains. Instead of making the community a passive recipient of a restoration project, the researchers want residents to help create the very baseline against which the river's future will be measured. When rituals become a source of pollution In 2022, when Sneha first visited the Tamiraparani for her PhD fieldwork, she encountered something she had not expected. The river is perennial, meaning it flows throughout the year. Yet during the summer, when water levels were low, stretches of its banks were covered in discarded clothes. The waste was linked to a ritual that had become increasingly common over the preceding two decades. At Papanasam temple, people visiting from different parts of Tamil Nadu began discarding the clothes of deceased family members into the river, believing that the practice would help their loved ones reach heaven faster. Sneha recalls being particularly shocked by where this was happening. The Tamiraparani emerges from a forested landscape, passes through the Papanasam area and begins its journey through human settlements. The dumping was taking place almost immediately after the river emerged from the dam and entered the human landscape. "Not even a kilometre of peace is the river getting, and it's just being dumped," she says. The problem is complicated by the fact that many residents do not practise this ritual themselves. Instead, the river receives waste from visiting pilgrims and tourists. In October this year, their grassroots dedication caught the attention of the world when The Iris Project named them winners of the 2026 Iris Prize. For the researchers, addressing this requires sensitivity. "When people have lost somebody, and they've come for this ritualistic relief in their mind, it's very sensitive to tell them not to dump clothes. They believe they're doing something for their loved ones, while not realising that they're actually polluting somebody else's backyard." There have been administrative interventions. Sneha recalls that former Tirunelveli district collector Vishnu Venugopal introduced bins and encouraged visitors to wash the clothes and dispose of them appropriately. While the practice has reportedly been prohibited, the waste accumulated over approximately two decades still needs to be removed. "Cleaning might take longer than it has taken to pollute it because that's the extent of the pollution," Sneha says. The team has also cleaned a one-kilometre stretch to understand what kinds of solid waste are entering the river. Among their findings were discarded shampoo, soap and hair-oil sachets. In the region's hot climate, where temperatures can reach 42 degrees Celsius, applying oil before bathing is a traditional practice. Small disposable packets make this convenient, but they also add to the river's plastic burden. The researchers are now exploring ways to reduce this waste. Can a river's future be protected by its youngest residents? For Sneha, one of the biggest lessons from previous conservation projects has been that restoration does not necessarily last. During her earlier work in Vadodara, her team cleaned a stream and helped bring crocodiles back to the area. But after she left the city for her PhD, she returned a few years later to find the stream had deteriorated again. The experience changed how she approached the Tamiraparani. "I work with people who belong to the landscape. So then it's basically their own backyards that they have to keep going back to," she says. That is also where Vidhya's involvement becomes central. Sneha and Vidhya recall how older residents sometimes welcome the young researchers as though they were their granddaughters. As someone from the region, she helps the team engage with residents, translate conversations and make the research accessible to local communities. “The biggest thing I've learned is that a river can be ‘read’ and everyone reads it differently. Farmers read it through the clouds. Fishers read it through the fish when they're there, and when they aren't. Everyone has their own way of knowing the river… they know when something is wrong. Nobody taught them this in a classroom. It comes from living beside the river every single day. That's why telling the stories of rivers, and of the people who live with them, matters so much to me. A river isn't just water and data. It's a part of people's daily lives, and when we listen, we start to see it the way they do,” she tells The Better India . Sneha and Vidhya recall how older residents sometimes welcome the young researchers as though they were their granddaughters. “Communities genuinely want to protect and conserve their river, but they often feel overwhelmed when the conversation turns into charts, numbers and technical words. We're working as a bridge between the community and the data,” Vidhya shares. The team has also begun taking this approach beyond the Tamiraparani. Since October 2025, it has conducted workshops to train young people in river monitoring and conservation . Around 40 students have been trained so far, including participants from Tirunelveli and other parts of India. Sneha hopes that the team will grow beyond its current seven members and encourage more young people to take responsibility for their own ecosystems. The training follows three levels. The first introduces participants to the different parts of a river, from its mouth and estuary to pools, rapids and riffles. The second covers water-quality parameters and their significance for human health and aquatic life. The third introduces policy and advocacy, helping participants understand how to communicate ecological concerns to local authorities. "We are developing a toolkit which makes it easy to understand how a river is monitored," Sneha says. "You don't need to be from a science background. We can train them. We have the resources to train them." Ultimately, Sneha hopes that the team will grow beyond its current seven members and encourage more young people to take responsibility for their own ecosystems. The world is looking at their approach In October this year, their grassroots dedication caught the attention of the world when The Iris Project named them winners of the 2026 Iris Prize. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Iris Project (@theiris_project) The Iris Prize is a global award created to find and trust young environmental leaders aged 14 to 24 who are actively protecting nature in their own backyards. Rather than favouring large institutions, the prize prioritises youth-led projects, especially from the Global South, where young changemakers hold genuine decision-making power and combine local action. Winning the flagship tier brought the RE-Verse Initiative a $15,000 unrestricted grant, placing their work on the Tamiraparani alongside fellow 2026 winners building tree-planting robots in Portugal and crafting eco-friendly school desks in Ghana. A river is more than the water it carries The Tamiraparani supports nearly 40,000 hectares of farmland. It sustains settlements, livelihoods, biodiversity and cultural practices across its course. But its future must also be understood through the fish that inhabit it, the otters that once moved along its banks, the plants that hold its ecosystem together, the communities that depend on it and the memories of people who remember when its water tasted different. The RE-Verse Initiative is still building its baseline. Recognising the Tamiraparani as a river with rights is only the beginning. Ensuring those rights are reflected in how people use, govern and care for it will require sustained participation, scientific evidence and institutional support. Its changing condition can be documented before the damage becomes irreversible. Its communities can become its observers and custodians. And one day, perhaps, the old man's memory of sweeter water will be more than just a recollection. All Picture Source: Sneha Shahi

items.title: I CAN Earthshot Challenge | How TN Students Turned Old Newspapers Into Waste Bags and Won $2,000
items.blurb: At a school in Ammaiyappan, Thiruvarur district, a discarded newspaper found a new purpose. Instead of being thrown away, it was folded into a waste bag, fitted with jute handles and coated with melted crayons to make it resistant to moisture. The idea was to offer households an alternative to polythene bags while addressing another problem: the difficulty of managing mixed waste. The students behind the initiative, called Decom POSSIBLE, have now won the 'Build a Waste-Free World' category at the inaugural I CAN Earthshot Challenge, earning a $2,000 grant to further develop their work. The project is developed by students of SSATN Panchayat Union Middle School in Ammaiyappan (West), Tamil Nadu. Turning discarded paper into an alternative The bags were made using materials that were readily available to the students. Old newspapers formed the main body, while jute was used for the handles. Discarded crayons were melted and applied as a coating to help the bags withstand moisture. The students took the idea beyond the school premises. Over a period of more than 30 days, they visited households, distributed the bags and spoke to residents about waste segregation. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Earthshot Prize (@earthshotprize) The initiative was designed to address mixed waste disposal as well as the challenges sanitation workers face when handling waste that has not been separated at source. But the students' work did not stop with the bags. A composting pit at school, and a community centre revived At the school, the team established a composting pit measuring 8 feet long, 2 feet wide and 3 feet deep. Organic waste, once separated from other household and school waste, was placed in the pit and converted into manure within a month. This gave the students a way to demonstrate what happens when biodegradable waste is kept separate instead of being mixed with plastic and other discarded mater The initiative also extended to an existing community facility. Within two weeks, the students helped revive a previously inactive community composting centre, creating another avenue for processing organic waste locally. The challenge invited children between nine and 17 years to identify environmental problems in their communities and develop solutions that could be put into practice. Photograph: (Earthshot Prize) The project reports that its activities have benefited 502 people. It also led to a response from the local panchayat: following the initiative, the panchayat announced that waste would have to be separately segregated before collection from 1 October 2026. This local policy change is an important part of the project. Household-level segregation depends not only on residents separating their waste, but also on collection systems that maintain that separation. When wet and dry waste are mixed again during collection, much of the effort made at home can be undone. From a school initiative to a national platform Decom POSSIBLE was among 15 finalist projects selected for the inaugural I CAN Earthshot Challenge. The finalists represented nine Indian states and Delhi, and their projects addressed five environmental priorities: protecting and restoring nature, reviving rivers, lakes and oceans, cleaning the air, building a waste-free world and fixing the climate. The challenge was organised by The Earthshot Prize in partnership with Alana and Design for Change. It invited children between nine and 17 years to identify environmental problems in their communities and develop solutions that could be put into practice. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Earthshot Prize (@earthshotprize) The other winning projects included a low-cost cooling crate developed by students in Punjab to keep vegetables fresh in hot conditions, biodegradable diyas designed to reduce pollution in the Godavari in Maharashtra , and a natural-material air filter developed by students in Bengaluru. For the students in Ammaiyappan, the next step is to keep the practices going beyond the award. According to the project details published by The Earthshot Prize, they plan to encourage more households to adopt composting and take the model to neighbouring schools and panchayats. Their next challenge will be to sustain these practices and encourage more households to adopt them. Sources: ‘Discover the Winners of the Inaugural I CAN Earthshot Challenge’ : Published on 22 October 2026 ‘The Earthshot Prize, Alana and Design for Change Announce Finalists of Nationwide I CAN Earthshot Challenge’ : By NewsVoir, Published on 23 October 2026

The day Birungi Nembe was born in a hospital in Bunia, in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, her mother, Sylvie Bongerize Tibasima, 46, was diagnosed with Ebola. Sylvie died a week later, leaving behind her husband and nine children, including her newborn daughter.

But the little girl had contracted the virus shortly after birth as well. Two weeks later, in early September, her tiny body was placed in a wooden coffin, which was nailed shut and lowered into a small grave by a burial worker dressed in protective gear. Few relatives attended; the risk of infection was just too high.

items.title: ‘I Became Six Characters at Once’: A 10-YO Gives the Panchatantra and Mahabharata His Own Voice Through a Free Audio Library
items.blurb: Note: The Vyasa Project does not publicly disclose the names of children who contribute to its platform. The child featured in this story has therefore been identified by their chosen nickname. For a Class 5 student (nickname Super_Goalie) at Royal Concorde International School in Bengaluru, narrating a story meant becoming six different people at once. One of the stories the young reader chose was Arjuna and the Bird's Eye from the Mahabharata. Having heard it from their parents several times, the child knew the story well. But recording it for other children offered a new experience: bringing each character to life with a different voice. "I particularly enjoyed this one because I could use different voices for the five Pandavas and their guru, Dronacharya. It felt like I could become six different people all at once," he shares. "I had heard this story from my parents many times, so I already knew it well. But this time, I got to tell it in my own way and add my own style." For the child, it was an opportunity to have fun with a familiar story. But with every page read aloud and every recording made, children are also practising their reading, exploring expression and becoming more comfortable with their own voices. A Class 5 student brings characters from the Mahabharata to life by narrating ‘Arjuna and the Bird's Eye’ in different voices for other children. This is the idea behind The Vyasa Project, a free, non-profit audio library where children narrate stories for other children. The initiative brings together two simple pleasures: reading a good story and listening to another child tell it. Its founders hope that this experience will encourage more children to pick up books, enjoy reading and discover the confidence that comes with expressing themselves. When children become storytellers The process begins with children exploring a curated collection of stories on the Vyasa Project platform. They can choose from Panchatantra tales, Aesop's fables, folktales, abridged classics and poems. The collection includes stories in English, Hindi, Telugu, Bangla and Kannada and Marathi, allowing children to explore narratives in languages they are comfortable with. From the Panchatantra to Aesop's fables, the platform offers children a growing collection of stories they can read, narrate or simply listen to. Once they have chosen a story, children practise reading it before recording their narration. They can listen to their recordings, re-record them if needed, and submit them for review. Every submission is manually checked before being added to the library. If a recording cannot be published because of quality issues, the child receives detailed feedback to help improve it. The platform also has demonstration videos to help children and parents understand its features and navigate the process. For Karan S Kumar, co-founder of The Vyasa Project, the idea comes from his own childhood relationship with books. "I was the kind of child who always had a book open. Those stories took me to worlds I could never have reached otherwise, and somewhere along the way they shaped how I think, how I speak and how I see other people," he says. He wanted to bring that same sense of wonder to more children. The idea of children narrating stories for their peers became a way to make reading feel less like a lesson and more like a shared experience. "When a child narrates a story, something changes. They find their voice and their confidence, and they discover that what they have to say matters. And when another child listens, it feels less like being taught and more like a friend sharing something special," he adds. A library that grows with every child's voice The stories are selected to be age-appropriate, engaging and enjoyable, with interesting characters, humour, unexpected twists and meaningful themes. Priyanka Tadipatri, co-founder of the project, says the English collection began with stories from different storytelling traditions, including the Panchatantra, Arabian Nights, Grimm's fairy tales, Aesop's fables and Zanzibar tales. It also includes abridged works by authors such as Charles Dickens, Mark Twain, L Frank Baum and Oscar Wilde. Karan S Kumar and Priyanka Tadipatri, co-founders of The Vyasa Project, hope to make reading a shared experience by encouraging children to tell stories to their peers. The collection has since expanded into regional languages, with the founders hoping to add more Indian and international languages over time. Importantly, children do not have to record stories to use the library. They can simply listen to narrations uploaded by other young readers and explore stories across genres and languages. The founders have also deliberately kept the platform free of likes, comments and peer-to-peer messaging. Their intention is to create an experience similar to visiting a library: children come to discover stories, enjoy them and return whenever they want to read or listen again. For Madurai Sridhar, a grandparent whose granddaughter regularly uses the platform, this interest has been particularly encouraging. "My granddaughter asks me to log in to The Vyasa Project regularly. What she loves most isn't the listening; it's reading stories aloud and recording them for other children. We're strict about screen time at home, and this is one of the few things on a screen I'm happy to say yes to," he says. He adds that seeing his granddaughter so absorbed in the activity has been reassuring, especially when children often move quickly from one activity to another. The early response has been encouraging. Within three months of starting the project, the team received close to 700 recordings across languages, with several children contributing more than 10 narrations each. Priyanka says they have also noticed children becoming more comfortable with narration after initially hesitating. Some begin tentatively but grow more confident within just a few paragraphs. A young reader records a story for The Vyasa Project, helping other children discover the joy of reading through listening. "We do not expect children to have perfect pronunciation or error-free submissions. For us, it is more important that they have fun, enjoy the journey and hopefully fall in love with stories and books," she says. Nischala Agnihotri, a working mother and children's author of Yellow Kabbadi , believes the value of reading extends beyond developing language and cognitive skills. "It's not just about cognitive skills. Reading as a habit works at a deeper level. It builds the unseen. It works on their character, personality, and how they develop their first response and thinking patterns," she says. She believes that folklore, poetry and storytelling traditions can play an important role in shaping how children understand the world. For her, The Vyasa Project is helping bring these experiences to more children. Making reading a shared experience To encourage more children to participate, The Vyasa Project is organising Readers' Quest 2026, a seven-day online storytelling challenge during National Library Week, from 14 to 20 November. Open to children in Grades 1 to 7, or those aged 6 to 12, the challenge invites participants to contribute at least seven narrations during the week. Up to 20 winners across junior and senior categories will receive prizes, certificates, and an opportunity to attend a Voice and Storytelling workshop led by RJ Jayashree Raj. But for the founders, the larger idea goes beyond a week-long challenge or the number of recordings in the library. With every story narrated, The Vyasa Project hopes to inspire another child to pick up a book and discover the joy of reading. As Karan puts it, "A child doesn't have to narrate a story to benefit from the platform. Listening is just as central to the experience." And perhaps that is what makes the idea special. One child discovers a story, another finds the courage to narrate it, and someone else listens and feels inspired to pick up a book. With every new voice added to the library, another child gets an invitation to discover a world between the pages. All images courtesy of Priyanka Tadipatri and The Blooming Dale School

items.title: WEIGHT IS A HEALTH STORY, NOT A JUDGEMENT OF WHO YOU ARE.
items.blurb: The shame belongs to stigma, not to the person asking for help. “Just eat less.” “Move more.” “You need more discipline.” Is weight mainly the result of personal choices? Not quite. Choices matter, but they operate within biology, genetics, appetite, environment, health conditions and access to support. Why does that distinction matter? Because blame can delay care. Obesity is recognised as a chronic, complex and relapsing disease. A better conversation doesn’t ask, “Why can’t you control your weight?” It asks how weight may be affecting health, and what realistic, evidence-led management support is available. So keep building habits that support you: balanced meals, regular movement, strength activity and good sleep. And speak to a qualified doctor about what support is appropriate for you. Asking for medical help is responsible care, not weakness, failure or cheating. Talk to a qualified doctor about your weight-management needs. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #WeightStigma #Obesity #WeightManagement #HealthNotJudgement [weight is not a character test, weight stigma, obesity is a chronic disease, willpower and weight, weight management support India]

items.title: How a Professor Turned Tamil Nadu’s Traditional Kolams Into a Computer Language
items.blurb: Early each morning in the month of Margazhi , a statistics professor would set out on his motorbike to watch women at work on their doorsteps. Gift Siromoney admired the kolams , but he was chasing a different question. How did women, many of them nonliterate, loop a line around a grid of dots, close it without error and repeat the feat from memory the next day? Working with his wife and fellow academic Rani Siromoney at Madras Christian College in Tambaram during the early 1970s, he concluded that the drawing follows rules precise enough to be written down as a formal grammar that a computer can run. A tradition older than the textbooks Every morning, women across Tamil Nadu sweep their thresholds, sprinkle them with water and cow dung, and trickle powder between their fingers to build symmetrical patterns, as the mathematician Marcia Ascher described in American Scientist in 2002. A kolam begins with a grid of dots called pulli , and tradition holds that the rice flour feeds ants and insects, so the day opens with an act of kindness. In the early 1970s, mathematician Gift Siromoney observed these drawings, curious about the rules guiding their creation. Siromoney traced the earliest mentions of kolam in Tamil literature to the 16th-century Madurai Meenakshiammai Kuram , followed by the 17th-century Thiru Kutraala Kuravanji . He also noted that older Tamil word lists, ancient paintings and travellers’ accounts say nothing about the art, so its documented literary history begins only in the 16th century. A red pen and seven sheets of carbon paper To see how a kolam grows, Siromoney devised a trick. He stacked seven sheets of paper, interleaved them with carbon paper, and asked practitioners to draw with a red ballpoint pen, removing the top sheet and its carbon at the end of each stage. Every sheet then showed earlier strokes in black and the newest stage in red, which gave him a frame-by-frame record of the drawing. Skilled practitioners always drew the pulli first and then built the pattern stage by stage in its natural segments, which suggested that they remembered kolams as chains of smaller units rather than as whole pictures. Practitioners and novices differed in how well they copied unfamiliar kolam patterns, so Siromoney treated kolam drawing as a learned skill. T Robinson of the college’s mathematics department adds that the women drew almost like the turtle moves of a programming language, with instructions such as go forward, turn left, and make a loop. How a folk art became a picture language With the computer scientist Kamala Krithivasan, the Siromoneys published ‘Picture languages with array rewriting rules’ in 1973 and ‘Array grammars and kolam ’ in 1974. Using seven sheets of paper and carbon copies, Siromoney documented how women built kolams, one stroke at a time. Their idea treated each kolam as a sentence in a pictorial language , where rules rewrite a small array of symbols into a larger one, much as grammar rules grow a sentence. Computer programs could then generate kolam patterns of a given type mechanically. Later researchers use these models, which they call Siromoney array grammars. The team also asked whether a pattern is made of one strand or several. For interlaced sikku kolam , Siromoney introduced operations called cut and join, which turn a single-strand pattern into a multi-strand one and back. Rani Siromoney and colleagues later noted that the same operations appear in the theory of circular DNA splicing. Why the discovery still matters For computer scientists, kolams supplied ready-made examples of existing picture languages and inspired new types, so a doorstep craft helped shape how machines draw and recognise images. None of this required the women to know any grammar. R Narasimhan, who worked alongside Siromoney, observed that a large share of practitioners were nonliterate and unaware that their designs have grammatical properties. The couple’s school of formal language theory at Madras Christian College, he wrote, became one of the best and most active in the field. The research continues. A 2018 paper by K G Subramanian, T Robinson and colleagues generated kolams using membrane computing, a model inspired by living cells, and showed that it can produce designs that earlier array grammars could not handle. Subramanian did that work in the college’s Department of Mathematics, so the research still runs from Tambaram. Kolams were one strand of a restless career. Siromoney also used computing to date medieval Tamil inscriptions, applied cluster analysis to sculptures at Mamallapuram and built what South First describes as the first teleprinter keyboard for Tamil. He died on 21 March, 1988, aged 56. Yet every Margazhi morning, the women whose hands inspired his grammar keep drawing, and the rules he glimpsed keep running quietly beneath their fingers. Sources ‘ Gift Siromoney, polymath who used AI concepts in the 80s to solve historical mysteries ’: by Poorani Balendra for South First, Published on 21 March, 2023 ‘ KOLAM ’: by T.
