items.title: ‘I Turned My MRI Into a Lotus Painting’: How Art Helped a PhD Scholar Fight Cancer & Paralysis
items.blurb: Even in the emergency room, Sapna Singh asked a nurse for a pen and paper. She wanted to draw. In the middle of a frightening medical emergency , art offered the 44-year-old something familiar to hold on to. Until then, she had been pursuing a PhD in the UK, building on years of work as an artist and teacher. Now, she was trying to make sense of a diagnosis that would change almost every part of her life. In February 2025, she began experiencing weakness in her left hand and leg. An MRI revealed a cancerous brain tumour, and a seizure soon left the left side of her body paralysed. She had moved to the UK with her 13-year-old son, Kabir, only a few months earlier. Her research was underway, and she had cleared her PhD proposal. Her attention shifted from her research and future plans to treatment and the demands of everyday life. After returning to India in April, she underwent brain tumour surgery. She had to relearn everyday movements and depend on others for tasks she had once managed without a second thought. Walking became a goal in itself, and even the easiest routines required patience. Through the uncertainty, however, she kept returning to her art. “Cancer made me a patient, but art reminded me that I was still Sapna,” she says. From failing an entrance exam twice to earning a PhD scholarship Her relationship with art began long before she imagined it would help her through an illness. Growing up in a joint family in Delhi, she spent much of her childhood drawing. By Class 9, she was making portraits, and when it came time to choose a subject in Class 11, she opted for painting. In September 2022, she enrolled in a master’s in design at Leeds Arts University in the UK, specialising in world-building and creature design. Turning that interest into a career took determination. She failed the entrance examination for Delhi’s College of Art twice, in 1999 and 2000. She tried again, secured admission in 2002, and went on to graduate in 2006, ranking second in her final year. She later completed a diploma in 3D animation and multimedia and began working in exhibition and stall design. Around 2008, she married Akshay Singh, an entrepreneur from Meerut. Over the following years, she continued to build her career while making room for family life. The family moved to Dubai in 2016, where she found new ways to work with art. She began teaching and taking private classes in 2017. Later, she joined Manipal Academy of Higher Education in Dubai, teaching animation, media, and communication. Teaching kept her connected to the creative world, but Sapna was not finished learning herself. In September 2022, she enrolled in a master’s in design at Leeds Arts University in the UK, specialising in world-building and creature design. She completed the course in a year, opening the door to another ambition. In 2024, she received a vice-chancellor’s scholarship to pursue a PhD at the University for the Creative Arts. Her proposed research focused on the impact of artificial intelligence on creative education and hiring in the industry. “Returning to education after so many years helped me rediscover my confidence and gave me a fresh motivation to keep learning,” she says. “I wanted to show myself that it is never too late to learn something new or chase a dream. For me, it was about much more than earning another degree. It was about giving myself the chance to begin again.” In October 2024, she moved to the UK with her son, while Akshay remained in Dubai for work and visited them frequently. She settled into her new life and began working towards her research. After years of studying, teaching, and finding her way into new areas of art, she was ready for the next chapter. A few months into her PhD, everything took an unexpected turn Around 10 February 2025, she noticed that her left hand and leg were becoming weak. Kabir was the first to pick up on the change. At the time, neither of them realised how serious it would turn out to be. “I thought it was something temporary and that she would soon be back to normal. I never imagined things would get this serious,” he says. She visited her general practitioner after a few weeks and was referred to Frimley Park Hospital. An MRI scan revealed a cancerous brain tumour. She was alone when she received the news. Her blood pressure rose, and she later suffered a seizure that left the left side of her body completely paralysed. The change was devastating. A woman who had spent years studying, teaching, travelling and managing her own life now faced the possibility of losing much of that independence. An MRI scan revealed a cancerous brain tumour. Soon, the family had to return to India for her treatment. She underwent brain tumour surgery at Fortis Hospital in Noida in April 2025, followed by chemotherapy, radiation, physiotherapy, rehabilitation, and anti-angiogenesis therapy. As treatment progressed, she had to adjust to a very different daily routine. Moving from her bed to a wheelchair, bathing, dressing, and using the toilet all required help. She also experienced fatigue and vertigo, while problems with her vision made some activities more difficult. For a period, her right eyelid remained closed. Although it has gradually opened, medication can still leave her vision blurred . The physical challenges were difficult, but losing the freedom to manage her own life took an emotional toll, too. “The hardest part was losing my independence. I went from managing my own life to needing help with basic everyday tasks. That change affected not only my body, but also the way I saw myself,” she tells The Better India . Akshay had to adjust, too. Before her illness, his wife was fiercely independent. She travelled on her own, pursued her studies, taught, and managed family responsibilities. Now, he was helping her through the most basic parts of the day while also caring for Kabir and keeping up with work. He cooked fresh meals to take to the hospital and spent as much time as he could with Sapna. Leaving her alone in the ward at night was especially hard. “There were moments when I would look at her and think, ‘How did our life change so much, so quickly?’” he says. He wanted to make things easier for her, but he also understood that help could not replace what she had lost. For her, being able to do things for herself had always been important. “You want to help, but you also know that the thing she wants most is not help. She wants her independence back,” he adds. Regaining that freedom has been a slow but consistent process. At first, she needed four people to help her walk. Over time, that number came down to three, then two, and eventually one. She has recently managed a few steps without support. She has also progressed from using a bedpan to a portable commode and later to using the toilet with assistance. These changes have taken time, and recovery has come with its share of complexities. Still, each improvement has given her something concrete to work towards. “I coped by focusing on very small improvements rather than thinking too far ahead,” she explains. When an MRI scan became a painting of a lotus Even before she knew what her recovery would look like, Sapna had found a way to cope with the uncertainty. During the medical emergency, she continued sketching, keeping her materials close by. She represented the tumour as a lotus, a flower she associated with wisdom and awakening. “In the emergency room, I asked a nurse for a pen and paper to draw. It was just my coping mechanism to take my thoughts away from the uncertainty and chaos,” she says. Her right hand, the one she used for painting and writing, remained functional. That gave her a way to return to a familiar part of herself, even as other parts of her life felt unfamiliar. Drawing also allowed her to express feelings that were difficult to put into words, from fear and frustration to loneliness, hope, and gratitude. One painting was based on her own brain MRI. She represented the tumour as a lotus, a flower she associated with wisdom and awakening. The scan that had delivered frightening news became the subject of a work she could interpret in her own way. Painting was not always easy . Her vision problems made it harder to work with fine details, which had been an important part of her practice. Rather than stop, she began adapting her approach, experimenting with patterns and finding different ways to create. Akshay has watched her work around these limitations. For him, seeing her paint is a reminder that her identity extends beyond her illness. “When she paints, I see her reconnecting with the person she has always been, not just the patient she has become,” he says. He has seen how difficult it can be for her to work when her vision is affected, but also how determined she is to find another way. “For an artist, whose work depends so much on observation, detail, colour, and visual control, this could have easily become another reason to stop. But she did not stop. Instead, she adapted,” he says. Art has not removed the challenges of recovery, but it has given Sapna a way to keep expressing herself while she works through them. She has continued painting and has also started writing about the turning points in her life, including the difficult moments she has experienced during treatment. Her son has seen how much effort this takes. Kabir, now in Class 8, notices the small changes in her recovery as well as her strength to keep working. “Nowadays, she can open her right eyelid and manages to eat by herself,” he says. For her son, these changes are part of seeing his mother gradually regain some of the abilities she had lost. He has also watched her continue to work towards her goals, even when recovery has made everyday life harder. “Art has become a kind of therapy for my mother during her recovery. Even with all the challenges she faces, she continues to paint, write her autobiography, and plan exhibitions. She is determined to see her dreams through, and watching her keep going has been inspiring for all of us,” he says. That aspiration has already taken her back to an exhibition. In March 2026, she participated in a four-day College Mate exhibition at a gallery near Parliament House in Delhi. After months of treatment and rehabilitation, it gave her the chance to share her work with an audience again. Art has not removed the challenges of recovery, but it has given Sapna a way to keep expressing herself. She is now planning a solo exhibition and hopes to publish an autobiographical book. Alongside these projects, she wants to return to her research and complete the PhD she began in the UK. Learning to measure progress differently Sapna’s recovery is still underway. She continues to need help with everyday activities, and walking independently remains a goal. Fatigue and vision problems can also limit what she is able to do on some days. Her life is not the one she imagined when she moved to the UK in 2024. But she is finding ways to make space for the things that matter to her, even as she learns to live with the changes brought on by her illness. Her husband says her ambitions have not disappeared with the changes to her physical abilities. “Her body has gone through a huge change, but her dreams, inquisitiveness, and zeal are still very much alive,” he says. “Her circumstances have changed, but she has not lost herself.” For her, moving forward does not mean pretending that the past year has been easy or expecting herself to return to the person she was before her diagnosis. It means allowing recovery to take the time it takes, while continuing to work towards the things she still hopes to do. She wants to regain more independence, return to research, and keep creating. Some days are spent focusing on her health; on others, she paints or writes. The progress may be slower than she once expected, but she is learning to recognise it on its own terms. “This experience has taught me that starting over does not always mean beginning from zero. Sometimes it means continuing from a completely different place, with a different body, different circumstances, and a different understanding of life,” she says. She knows that recovery cannot be rushed and that the plans she once made may take longer to realise. For now, she is learning to measure progress on her own terms. “Your timeline may change, but that does not mean you have to abandon your dreams. Give yourself permission to move slowly and redefine what progress looks like,” she says. Sapna still has a long way to go in her recovery, and the PhD remains a goal she hopes to return to. There is no definite timeline for what comes next. Sapna still has a long way to go in her recovery, and the PhD remains a goal she hopes to return to . Right now, she is taking things one step at a time, making art when she can and putting her experiences into words. “I am still learning, creating, and hoping. For me, that itself is a form of moving forward,” she says. All pictures courtesy Sapna Singh.

items.title: Stubble to Mushrooms? How is it even possible?
items.blurb: ndia burns millions of tonnes of paddy straw every year. But what if this agricultural waste could grow mushrooms instead? At ICAR-National Rice Research Institute in Cuttack, scientists are helping farmers explore mushroom cultivation using paddy straw. Fungi break down tough plant fibres, allowing farmers to turn straw into growing beds for paddy straw mushrooms. According to a 2022 ICAR study, cultivating 4,000 mushroom beds annually could generate ₹3 lakh in net income, with leftover material potentially adding another ₹1.36 lakh through vermicomposting. But this isn’t a magic fix for stubble burning. These mushrooms need temperatures of 30–35°C, while poor-quality spawn, contamination, limited markets and food-safety risks remain serious challenges. Scientists estimate this method could handle only 8–12% of a region’s straw burden. Mushroom farming won’t end stubble burning on its own. Forget the smell. You could almost taste the Madeleines. Those late nights in Brussels from 10 years ago when time had lost all meaning. So it seemed it might be on Friday. A press conference scheduled for 12.30pm pushed back a quarter of an hour. And then another 15 minutes. Yet another 15 minutes. There are few things the EU does better than taking negotiations down to the wire.

But there the similarities ended. Because when the presser eventually started about an hour later than planned, everything was sweetness and light. António Costa, president of the European Council, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Andy Burnham presented themselves as the perfect throuple. It had been love at first sight, and they couldn’t wait for their next tryst. They could barely take their eyes off one another. items.title: UK says reset deal with EU agreed but talks will continue ‘in some areas’ – live
items.blurb:
Statement from UK comes after EU said deal would not take effect without future agreement over university tuition fees

Senior correspondent

Making today’s reset deal contingent on a further agreement on the level of tuition fees for EU citizens is designed to neutralise the leverage London gets in the next six months, EU sources have said.

Senior diplomats had already confirmed this week that the EU would defer the deal on the level of tuition fees for another six months, a move designed to give the UK leverage in parallel negotiations to have the UK included in Made in Europe legislation designed to protect EU supply chains against China.

But the move to make the food and drink deal also contingent on a tuition fees deal effectively seeks to neutralise the leverage the UK gets today.

This is a serious chess game and shows the EU, again, is willing to speak very warmly about the UK but will play absolute hard ball when it comes to conceding any points to a former member state.

It was the same point France was making last night insisting the UK could not have voting rights on legislation in relation to food and drink.

During his meeting with businesses in Brussels, PM Burnham said his EU deal would add up to 0.5% to the UK’s GDP.

“We’re pretty much there, and it’s a really good deal.”

“Treasury analysis out today is saying that now it’s clear up to 0.5% on GDP as a result of the deal. The single biggest growth intervention in this Parliament.”

items.title: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins
items.blurb:
In other countries, local communities have a say in their futures. If the UK were truly democratic, everywhere would be a parish in control of its own fate

Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections.

And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK.

Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist, author and BBC broadcaster. His book The Village in Britain: And Why Place Matters is published this month

items.title: While the headlines rave about Milburn’s Neets review, the young people I know are angry and frustrated | Felicity Halstead
items.blurb:
The focus seems to be on welfare reform as a way to deal with youth unemployment. But young people just want a fairer jobs market

  • Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity

I was at my desk last Thursday morning as a steady stream of young people filed into GoodWork’s central London community hub for a day of employability workshops. Despite the accusations of disengagement among young people, they didn’t need me to tell them that proposals to cut some benefits for under-25s were all over the news. I could hear them talking about it as soon as the lift pinged open – and the mood was low.

Alan Milburn has made a concerted effort to say that he doesn’t believe young people are to blame for dire levels of youth unemployment. He says the system has let them down and only a decade-long transformation will fix a problem that is complex and deeply entrenched. Simply recognising the scale of the problem and being willing to invest in a solution is a positive start.

Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity

items.title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers
items.blurb:
Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner

The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations.

Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica, has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate.

items.title: From Germany, with love: a letter to the UK | Klaus Brinkbäumer
items.blurb:
As Andy Burnham pushes to reopen Brexit, Berlin won’t say it, but the truth is, we just want you back

Dear British friends,

Germans are not the love-letter writing kind of people. When we write a letter, a complaint is usually not far off. But we cannot complain about you. About other things, yes: transatlantic relations, or Trump, ja, ja. Or our own chancellor, who every morning talks about reforms which, by the evening, we know will never get done. But when I think about Britain I feel only one thing: longing.

Klaus Brinkbäumer, a former executive editor at Der Spiegel, is an author and podcast and TV host in Germany
